The estimates
of the Department of Agriculture provide me with the opportunity of indicating to the committee the extent to which agriculture is a factor in the economy of Huron-Perth, and at the same time to indicate to the committee some of the problems that the farmers in that district are concerned with.
In contributing as he has done to the economy of the district, the farmer of Huron has at the same time increased the value of his farm plant and the stock which he owns. During the period 1931 to 1951 the value of livestock on Huron farms increased from $7,473,000 to $36,278,000, or five times as much. During the same period, the value of livestock across Canada increased less than four times. The situation at the time of the last census was that the county stood first in the province of Ontario with respect to its agricultural worth.
The farmers in Huron-Perth quite properly are concerned that an equitable balance be maintained between the return which they receive for their produce and the cost of the
Supply-Agriculture
products which must be purchased. There is, of course, a demand on the part of the consumer of food products for lower prices, and this is only natural. Unfortunately, however, the consumer in demanding lower prices sometimes tends to place the entire blame for the cost of food on the primary producer. In doing so, the consumer forgets that included in the price of the food he buys is an increasingly higher cost of grading, of packaging, of handling, of transportation. Certainly, no one can be critical of any regulation that ensures a proper quality or standard of cleanliness in food. At the same time, is it possible that on occasion the pure mechanics of distribution are considered as the end, rather than as a means to the end of putting food on the table of the consumer. It seems to me that this whole matter of the distribution and handling of food products could be explored quite profitably with the thought that practices or regulations may be found that have outlived their usefulness and that are only contributing to higher retail costs. If this situation does exist, it can only have the effect of lessening consumption and thus of lowering the return to the farmer.
As I pointed out, farmers quite properly are concerned lest the amount they receive for their product should get out of balance with the amount they are required to pay for the things they must buy. On this balance depends the standard of living the farmer enjoys. It may well be that a study of handling and distribution costs could result in eliminating unnecessary -costs, thereby making possible an increased return to the farmer.
Much has been said concerning markets for agricultural products which, it has been suggested, have disappeared. References of this nature are difficult to understand, when it is realized that Canada's export of farm products to more than 100 countries reached an all-time high of $1,213,595,000 in 1952. The situation is not that markets have been lost, but rather that emphasis has been placed on those markets that are in a position to return the highest possible price to the Canadian farmer.
One of the major factors in ensuring that the farm product continues to have profitable markets is the extent to which domestic demands are increasing. This was recognized at a recent meeting of the Ontario beef cattle producers' association. The Rural Cooperator, in its issue of April 14, 1953, reported the meeting as follows:
Surplus of beef is about 16 per cent of the total supply, which, in view of the increasing population and industrial expansion, is not too serious,

Supply-Agriculture
president B. B. Warniea, Barrie, told the recent annual meeting of the Ontario beef cattle producers' association.
In his annual report, Mr. Warniea expressed the opinion that it might not be too many years before Canadians would not be surplus producers of beef, or for that matter, of any agricultural products except wheat and barley.
An increase in the consumption of beef can be expected because of the increasing birth rate, increase in immigration and longer life expectancy.
All this indicates, I think, that the future of agriculture is not something about which we need be despondent. At the same time, there can be no grounds for complacency. Farmers in Huron-Perth, like farmers everywhere, quite properly demand that the economic climate in Canada be such that their net return is maintained at a level comparable to that being received in other industries and by other classes. That does not mean for one moment that the farmers of Huron-Perth are looking for handouts. Like their pioneer ancestors, who hewed from the lands of the Canada Company the homesteads which have become the splendid farms of Huron and Perth, the farmers of today are proud of their independence.
However, they do look for and are entitled to receive from government that support necessary to protect them from factors over which they have no control, such as weather and disease. A farmer has the right to expect his government to protect him from disaster. They insist on a continuation of the legislation of 1944 which, during the intervening years, has contributed so greatly to agricultural stability. They insist, too, that in the application of support legislation, a realistic approach be taken with respect to the amount of the support which is established, bearing in mind the prevailing cost of production, and also with respect to the selection of the products for which support is provided.
At the same time, I feel that farmers appreciate that support, at too high a level or at a level which has inherent in it a large element of profit, is but an invitation ultimately to some measure of control and, in the end, can be of no lasting benefit to the agricultural industry.
The success of agriculture must continue to be based on the vision and vigour of the individual farmer, coupled with an enlightened program of assistance made available to him by government. This combination will continue to have the effect of providing stability and overcoming those unknowns which for so many years in the past have beset agriculture.

Mr. Chairman, 1 intend to take only a few moments. It is not my

desire to get into the debate just for the sake of getting into it. But as no one from the maritime provinces has spoken about this question of agriculture, and no one has questioned the statements the Minister of Agriculture made the other day concerning the favourable conditions which primary producers are privileged to enjoy, I feel compelled to say just a few words on behalf of the farmers of my constituency.
The arguments to which I have listened thus far would seem to indicate that all the difficulties are located in Ontario and the prairie provinces, and that the farmers in the rest of Canada are quite happy. This is not a true picture. Speaking on April 27 the Minister of Agriculture said, as reported at page 4440 of Hansard:
Net income to farmers from the sale of farm products reached a peak of $2*2 billion in 1951. Estimates for the net income received in 1952 are placed at just under $2 billion. There is some indication that this present satisfactory position may be maintained. The cost of equipment and materials used in agricultural production reached a peak in 1952 and has declined since that time.
Then he went on to quote statistics to show that the decline was approximately 5 per cent.
A little later in his speech, in the second column on the same page, he made this reference to hogs:
Hog prices are maintaining reasonably well the advances made since the late war years. The average farm price for hogs for the years 1943 to 1945 was $16.63 per hundred pounds. This increased to an average of $27.27 for the years 1950 to 1952.
I presume the minister arrived at these figures from statistics, and I do not intend to quarrel with him about those statistics or enter into any argument concerning them. But averages, which may be the only yardstick to which he can refer, do not give a true picture of the situation of farmers generally; and that is the point I wish to make. The minister's suggestion cannot go unchallenged.
So far as the farmers are concerned, the test of prosperity is not found in the prices they receive for their products, on an average. I suggest a better test is the aggregate result as shown in the increase of wealth which the majority of farmers are able to show as the results of their work.
When averages are taken as the yardstick, then the average result can be obtained. when only a few farmers are doing well and, at the same time, the great majority are not doing well-in fact, are going behind. That is the situation which I say the agricultural producers in my constituency are facing, and it is a condition which I suggest applies generally throughout New Brunswick.

I do not intend to speak at length about this subject, but it would seem that the minister wishes to leave the impression, when he gives the average figures for hog prices, as they are set out in Hansard, that the hog producers are doing very well. The average price may have gone up, but as far as my constituency in New Brunswick is concerned the picture is entirely different. I ask the minister to go down and visit the farms there and he will find farm after farm with empty hog pens. Those farmers have been forced out of the hog business. Those who were able to stay in may be getting better prices, but the majority of farmers are not in the hog business.
At one time we in that part of our province had a prosperous hog-bacon business, but you cannot find that condition today. They have nearly all been forced out of business and that is why I say that that statement should not go unchallenged.
Then with regard to potatoes, I should like to quote again from the minister's statement as reported on page 4443 of Hansard of April 27. The minister said:

Those figures would indicate that during the last two years the potato growers must have been making a lot of money. If that were the true situation the minister would not be receiving telegrams, petitions and delegations of potato growers asking for some change in marketing conditions, for an extension of support prices and so on. If that average were true it would satisfy the farmers. The average for the first two years would indicate that the farmers lost considerable money.
The situation as it actually is, is that there are a few large potato growers. The majority of farmers are not potato producers. The large potato producer may make money year in and year out, but just take the year 1951-52 as an example. In the spring of 1952 many farmers were unable to put in potatoes even though the price was $10 per barrel. They found they had to sell what they would have otherwise liked to plant because of the high price.
Other farmers who may have grown a few potatoes did not receive that average price because they were obliged to sell during the fall when prices were much lower in order to pay their fertilizer and other bills which
Supply-Agriculture
they had run up during the summer to finance themselves during the crop year. The real picture is that there were only a few farmers who got those high prices which created the rather good-looking average.
The complaint of the farmers in my constituency, and I think this applies to New Brunswick generally, is that they are not getting a square deal. I think all I need to back up that statement is to say that around the country many farms are being vacated. Farmers are leaving their farms. It is not because they want to leave them, because the New Brunswick boys who have grown up on farms would like to stay there provided they could get a good return and have as bright prospects on the farm as there might be some place else.
The fact is that they cannot make money because of increased costs of production and increased cost of machinery. There may be a 5 per cent reduction in the cost of machinery, but that is immediately offset by the increases of 6 and 9 per cent in freight rates. This year our machinery will be no cheaper. As a result of these freight rates and tariffs barriers are being built up between the maritime provinces and our natural markets. Any increased cost of production must be borne by the producer, and as a result he receives less for the potatoes, hay, poultry and everything else he raises.
During the last six months many farmers have gone out of the poultry business even though the statement made by the minister would seem to indicate that our poultry men should be prosperous. We should look at the situation on the ground in order to see what is happening. Taxes are higher, the cost of living is higher, freight rates are higher and fertilizer is higher. The majority of farmers are not prosperous. They are not enjoying the general prosperity of this country. They are not getting the same deal that people in industry are getting. Many people are leaving New Brunswick to go to other parts of Canada because they believe they can get a better deal with shorter hours. They feel that they can do better for themselves and have more in the end.
We are losing a good class of people. There is no better place to live than in the maritimes and you will find no better people anywhere in this country. They are hardworking, industrious and reliable. I think they should get a little better deal. If the farmers get a better deal, then the great number of us who depend on the farmers will also get a better deal.
I shall not take up any more time of the committee, but I did feel that someone from

Supply-Agriculture
the maritimes should let the committee know that the farmers there are not enjoying the prosperity that should be theirs according to the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture. I think that statement was made in good faith and was based on statistics. I am not finding fault with the statement, but I do want to say that it does not apply to my constituency and to the maritime provinces generally.

Mr. Chairman, I have only one thing to say in reply to what has just been said. The hon. member started off by suggesting that I had generalized too much, that the situation was not the same in New Brunswick as it was elsewhere. That may be true, but in reply I would say that the hon. member has generalized too much with regard to New Brunswick. It is not so long since I was in New Brunswick to do a little checking for myself.
When the hon. member says that the hog pens in New Brunswick are all empty he certainly has not been looking around. There were 2,400 more hogs in New Brunswick last June than there were the preceding June. The hog population has not been going down; it has been going in the other direction. There were 86,400 hogs on farms in New Brunswick last June. The year previous there were 84,000. The present hog population in New Brunswick is just about as high as it has ever been.
It is not correct to say that the hog population has been going down in the last few years. The hog population there, as in other parts of Canada, went up during the last year as compared with the preceding year. It is up in New Brunswick as well as in other provinces, so that generalizing on statistics does apply in so far as hogs in New Brunswick are concerned.
I cannot accept that from the minister as being the fact. According to his information he is just about a year behind.

The only reason I did not give the figures for June, 1953, is that they are not available.
Mr. Her ridge: Mr. Chairman, the remarks of hon. members of all parties during the debate on this item indicate a growing concern on the part of farmers across Canada with markets and1 prices. Other members of our group have expressed very clearly the feelings of this group in that respect. I had an opportunity during a previous debate to express my views concerning the necessity for a wider application of the Agricultural Prices Support Act, particularly as far as soft

fruits, poultry and other products which are of particular interest to the farmers in the interior of British Columbia are concerned. Therefore very briefly I am going to take the time to deal with a problem with which this group is much concerned, as I am sure many other members of the house are. I refer to the problem of an over-all national agricultural conservation policy.
While at the present time farmers are naturally interested in the first instance in markets and prices, in our opinion the No. 1 long-range problem in Canada is the maintenance of soil fertility. The evidence is there from the Atlantic to the Pacific for anyone who wants to seek it. We see rundown farms in the maritimes and exhausted farms in central Canada. We see grain grown year after year on the prairies when other cultivation policies should be followed. I have personal knowledge of thousands of acres of impoverished orchard soil because of wrong agricultural practices, because of the excessive use of fertilizers and overcul-fivation and the failure to use enough green crops and manure.
I know there are two schools of thought. There are the organic farmers who believe in nothing but manure and green crop farming, and there are those who place too much emphasis upon chemical fertilizers. I am of the opinion that a proper balance should be struck between the two. We have had in the interior of British Columbia for some years a disease known as the little cherry disease which has been proven to be caused by a virus. I have grown fruit for over forty years and I maintain that basically it is caused by a condition in the soil. I am beginning to think that evidence is being produced to support my view and the view of a good number of growers. I know of trees that have produced little cherries for ten years and are now producing excellent crops of cherries. I think that is because there is an improved condition in the soil that allows the cherry tree to overcome the virus just as a person overcomes tuberculosis because they are healthy. In my opinion the crux of the question of maintenance of soil fertility in Canada lies in the maintenance of soil fibre content.
We in this group are very much interested in the development of an over-all agricultural conservation policy. We give credit to the minister's department for the good work that has been done under P.F.R.A. in the prairie provinces. There is no question about it. Everyone knows that the work that has been done by that branch has been of great value to the people directly concerned and of great

value to Canada as a whole. We believe that the P.F.R.A. provisions should be extended to all provinces in Canada, that the principles are sound and that the same benefits should be extended to all provinces.
In addition, I understand that some years ago the government had a system of cash subsidies for fibre producing plantings. I am very much intrigued with that sort of subsidy rather than a direct subsidy possibly at the price level in some instances. I believe in a subsidy at the source for the planting of fibre producing crops or for agricultural practices that increase the fertility of the soil. I know that in the old country a check of farms is even made as to the tons of manure distributed and the amount of oil cake meal fed to the stock. All these factors are taken into account even when fixing the rent. The farmer who plants fibre producing crops, who uses oil cake meal and high protein feeds for his cattle and who spreads manure on his farm and turns in green crops gets a deduction from his rent because he is actually increasing the value of the farm while he is farming. I think we have got to establish an interest in that sort of thing in this country. I suggest to the minister that consideration be given to some sort of subsidy at the source for fibre producing plantings and for conservation policies generally which it has been proved will increase the productivity of the soil.
I also suggest that the minister's department should give some consideration to the exemption from income taxation of capital expenditures that actually increase the productivity or fertility of farms. That is given consideration in some other countries, and in that way I think that form of subsidy is on a very sound foundation, and is a form of subsidy that will do something to improve the whole position of agriculture generally throughout the years.
I should like to say a word or two about sugar beets. The hon. member for Lethbridge is one of the leading champions of the sugar beet industry in the house, and we give him credit for the work he has done in that respect. Members of this group are interested in the problems of the sugar beet growers and the wider aspects of the question as it affects Canada as a whole. I want to read a letter on the matter at this point because I am one of those persons who fundamentally are very sympathetic to farmers. I am a peasant farmer myself. I have lived on the land all my life, and therefore I am naturally interested in people who struggle to make a living from the soil. But the
Supply-Agriculture
things that are done against the interests of the farmer unconsciously, shall I say, are amazing. I had my wife go into three or four stores in Ottawa to buy sugar. I told her to ask the storekeepers whether, when buying sugar for canning, sugar produced from sugar beets is as good as that produced from cane sugar. Every shopkeeper said that cane sugar was better. That is the result of false propaganda.
In addition, I have talked to members of the house who are of the opinion that in sweetening quality cane sugar is superior to beet sugar. I have also talked to commercial travellers for grocery firms who are under the same impression. That caused me to write a letter to Dr. C. A. Morrell, director of the food and drug divisions, because I was confident in my own mind that that was not true. In fact I knew it was not true but I wanted evidence from a recognized authority. I wrote to Dr. Morrell, told him of my experience, and this is his reply under date of February 20, 1953:
Dear Mr. Herridge:	*
I have your letter of February 18 inquiring about the chemical qualities and sweetening value of sugar manufactured from sugar cane and sugar beets.
According to the scientific texts available to me on sugar technology and to the best of my knowledge, the granulated sugar manufactured from sugar cane and sugar beet has exactly the same composition and sweetening value. In fact, the product is 99'5 per cent or better pure chemical sucrose. Brown sugar, or yellow sugar, which is made by partial refinement of the juice of the sugar cane or sugar beet, contains 90 per cent or more of sucrose, less than 1-5 per cent of ash, and less than 4-5 per cent moisture. This product would have the same sweetening value when manufactured from sugar cane or sugar beet. There may be a slight difference in the composition of the ash. Fruit canned with sugar (sucrose) manufactured from sugar beets, providing equivalent amounts are used, would keep as long as fruit canned from sugar (sucrose) manufactured from sugar cane.
I put that on the record because I think we should do what we can to contradict the misinformation with which our housewives and consumers are supplied. In that respect, when considering the sugar beet industry and its value in the Canadian economy, I think we cannot entirely view it on a dollars and cents basis as regards cost of production and the cost of bringing in a ton of sugar from some other country. We have got to consider what part the sugar beet industry can play in the maintenance of soil fertility throughout the country. There is no question about it, where sugar beets are grown farmers are improving the fertility of their farms every year.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in that connection I just want to quote from a book that was

handed to me, "Through the Leaves", September-October, 1950, issue, page 11:
Unless a farmer can affirmatively answer the question "To feed or not to feed?'' he sooner or later must answer the question "To farm or not to farm?" This is true because farming requires manure and manure comes from feeding. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I say in connection with this whole subject that when considering subsidies for soil fibre plantings or considering the beet industry in Canada you have also got to consider the contribution made to the improved fertility of our farms and the raising of the fibre content. I wish to devote my remarks entirely to one subject that has been under discussion here before but which is the special interest of all Canadians without regard to the part of the country from which they come. I think there are many hon. members in this house who were both shocked and surprised when they heard the letter read by the Minister of Agriculture which purported to be a letter delivered to the premier of the province of Saskatchewan. Actually, we are informed, it had not been delivered at the time it was read in this house; however, that is a mere detail.
Your information is wrong if you were so informed, because it was delivered before I read it.
I am informed of that statement in this house and if the statement made by the hon. member is incorrect then the minister can correct that on the record.

I corrected it last evening
when you were not here.

The time of delivery does not
change the effect of this letter, the timing of Which was so obvious that no comment is necessary.
The South Saskatchewan river development project is not something of limited and exclusive interest to the people of Saskatchewan any more than the St. Lawrence

deep waterway and power project is a subject of exclusive interest to the people of Ontario and Quebec. Hon. members have indicated in this house their interest in and, generally, their support of the St. Lawrence deep waterway as a project which is of national interest. The South Saskatchewan river development project comes in the same category although it is not as large a project. Nevertheless, in relation to the economy of Saskatchewan the South Saskatchewan river development project is just as important as the St. Lawrence deep waterway is to the province of Ontario. Both are important to the economy of Canada as a whole as well as to the local areas involved.
The letter which was read in this house on April 27, as reported in Hansard at page 4444, is a surprising communication after this subject has been under discussion for so many years. In that letter the minister, speaking on behalf of the government, says this to the government of the province of Saskatchewan:
. . . I am authorized by my colleagues to discuss such a proposal with you once the question of water rights has been settled among the three prairie provinces and agreement reached that the water would be available for the project.
Did this government, Mr. Chairman, tell the government of the province of Ontario that it would be ready to discuss the St. Lawrence deep waterway after all the other agreements had been completed?
Certainly they did.

Of course not. We know perfectly well that they have not all been completed yet, and we know perfectly well that they could not be completed until the dominion government made its fundamental and basic decision. The government has not hesitated to make its position quite clear in regard to the St. Lawrence deep waterway, without referring it to a royal commission. Although the government has in this case insisted upon the additional information which would be available from a royal commission beyond what was already available through its own engineers, it now invites the Saskatchewan government to provide the information which it has apparently failed to obtain over all these years.
Then let us examine carefully the second last paragraph of the letter, and I quote:
Any proposal would, of course, have to include some satisfactory means of determining in advance what the total cost of the project would be, and what the federal share of the cost would be.
This would be essential so that there was no open-ended commitment which might result in the final cost being far greater than anything either government would regard as reasonable.

Mr. Chairman, this late profession of virtue is unfortunately not appropriate in this case. Already the government has spent a great deal of money to obtain information which it now apparently seeks from the government of the province of Saskatchewan. The government has also gone still farther. The government of Saskatchewan communicated with the Prime Minister in a telegram which is contained in the Hansard of yesterday at page 4551. In that telegram the government of Saskatchewan states that the government of Canada has been informed that the government of Saskatchewan is prepared to enter into agreement in regard to this project. Without going into the full telegram I do want to refer to the reply under yesterday's date, and I will simply quote the last sentence of the telegram sent by the Prime Minister of Canada to the premier of the province of Saskatchewan as it appears at page 4552 of Hansard:
Before deciding whether and to what extent the federal government should participate we must know what would be involved and to what extent the provincial government is willing to accept these conditions.
In other words, after all these years the dominion government still leaves it uncertain as to whether it is ready to proceed with this project at all. Now, Mr. Chairman, it is time this pretence, this tawdry and cynical pretence, came to an end.
That is what they call an open-ended commitment.

Yes, that is an open-ended
commitment for political purposes to evade the decision which should have been made long ago.
Let us see what was said on behalf of this government by a member of the government, and I will quote the words of the minister who is primarily responsible when he spoke on behalf of the government as far back as 1946:
The dominion government had already mapped out a program, and it was a program involving $110 million. This would be used largely in providing for the storage of water and partly for the distribution of this water where needed.
There is no uncertainty there. This was a project that was to be proceeded with.
That is not a reference to the South Saskatchewan river project.
Of course it is involved.

It is one of four projects
estimated to cost $110 million.

Then let me refer to what the minister said on behalf of the government in the summer of 1948:
... a decision would be reached on where the dam on the South Saskatchewan should be placed.

No conditions are mentioned there; there is no mention of any request to the government of the province to find out what the cost was going to be so that the government, with its virtuous approach to these things, would have no open-ended commitments.

Over and over again, in answer to requests that some positive statement be made with regard to this project in which every Canadian is interested-just as we are interested in the St. Lawrence deep waterway, the causeway to Cape Breton island or any other project of that kind which is for the general advancement of the economy of Canada-we were told that the government was waiting to obtain information from a royal commission, not from the government of Saskatchewan.
Mr. Chairman, let us hope that evasion of this kind will not be accepted by anyone in this committee. We have a right to know what the government has decided to do upon the basis of information obtained at considerable expense to the taxpayers of Canada. A number of us have indicated our belief that this project should be proceeded with and that the undertaking by the dominion government should be given immediately. We believe that this is more than merely a matter of local concern. We believe that this development in the heartland of the great province of Saskatchewan would not only bring development there but would raise the whole economy of that province, and, incidentally, would give to the people of Saskatchewan a feeling of confidence that the people of the rest of Canada, as represented by the members of this parliament, share their concern about the economy of that province. Some of us share the views ex-

the information which was obtained at the expense of the taxpayers. Many of us felt that it could act upon the advice and the information available from the engineers employed by the government. Mr. Chairman, I repeat that this is not a matter of exclusive interest and concern to the people of Saskatchewan. Whether we come from the east or from the west, as Canadians we are interested in the advancement of the whole Canadian economy. No matter what has happened already, I hope the government will now stop this evasion, will make a definite and unequivocal statement that it is prepared to proceed, and upon that basis will obtain the necessary agreements with the provincial governments that are indicated in a case of this kind.

Mr. Chairman, during the discussion of the first item of the agricultural estimates, when hon. members were not discussing matters pertaining to one of the provinces, we have heard some discussion regarding markets, or in some cases the lack of markets. I think it must be generally admitted that there are only two natural markets open to Canadian agriculture. One of course is our home market and the other

is the market in the country to the south of us. The reason for this is that our costs of production have resulted in what has been referred to in this house as our "pricing ourselves out of the market"; or, to be more objective, "we have priced ourselves out of the British market."
By a system of offering to buy surpluses of certain farm products at a figure that in effect was a price support program, the government has prevented the collapse of any branch of agriculture. By regulating the entire economy of the country so that employment has been kept at an unheard-of peak, the government has provided Canadian farmers with a home market that has been absorbing almost everything we have produced, with the exception of wheat. After all there is no security like a steady job, and the families who are employed are generally good spenders. These are the people who have provided us with our best markets over the last number of years. I do not think anyone can successfully refute that statement.
The people of the United States are the only other people in the world who enjoy our standard of living and who have our kind of money. To my mind, under ordinary conditions that country is the most accessible outlet for nearly all our surpluses. However, since the change of government there we must admit that the future of our marketing in that country is perhaps not too bright.
Having in mind the fact that we have fairly high prices according to other countries, I believe that the one feature of Canadian agricultural products that will help to sell them is quality. Particularly is this true of pork products. I have always believed that the production of a good quality product should be encouraged, and because the spread at the present time between the price of a grade A hog and a grade B1 hog is only 40 cents per hundredweight, or an average of 60 cents per hog, I believe the grades under which hogs are sold should be revised and a much greater spread in price made available to the farmer who takes the time and trouble to produce grade A hogs. In my opinion he should receive at least $4 more for his hog. As a step in this direction I would suggest that the present government bonus of $2 for grade A hogs should be increased by at least $1.
That was the bonus which was in effect in Ontario when the Ontario government was paying a bonus of $1 for grade A hogs. A couple of years ago that government ceased to pay that bonus and since that time we have had only the federal subsidy.
I think the present support price for hogs is a reasonable approach to the situation. It is interesting to note that on Tuesday of

this week hogs in Toronto were quoted at $29.50 whereas on the same day a year ago they were quoted at $26. It is also interesting: to note that hogs have sold in Toronto at 23 cents for only a short period in February. I think that was due to a drastic change in the system of selling hogs in Ontario. The result was that for a week or so it was difficult to establish a market, but as soon as buyers and sellers became adjusted to the new systern the price has been rising, until this week it is $29.50.
There is another product that is produced in considerable volume in my district, and I refer to butter. I think the government should be commended for its action in establishing a floor price of 58 cents per pound for butter for the next two years. I think that action is generally being well received by the cream producers throughout the country. I have here a copy of a letter which was sent to the right hon. minister by the federation of agriculture in my county in which they thank him for the floor price under butter for the next two years.
I should like to discuss for a minute or two the situation that exists at the Ontario stock yards in Toronto. Under regulations of the federal health of animals branch it has been impossible for several years, while the province was being tested county by county for t.b., to remove cattle from these yards back to the farms without having them needled and kept isolated for three days until government veterinarians could check for reactors. Any animal that showed dairy type was held in the testing barn at the yards for three days and then released.
Ontario has now all been tested and every county declared an accredited area and it seems to me that there is no valid reason why the Ontario stockyards should not also be declared an accredited area and the free movement of cattle allowed in and out. I think this would be only fair because for a long time I have felt that the onus for delivering clean cattle should rest with the seller. Up to the present time the buyer has suffered the loss if he had a reactor and he received no compensation except the carcass value. Any person who has handled these cattle knows that the carcass value of a light stocker is pretty small, having regard to the price that is paid on the hoof.
Having these stocker and feeder cattle tested at Winnipeg would mean a large saving to the department in veterinarian fees alone. I know in my own little business I have bought cattle for farmers, and as I live near the boundaries of four counties, in one truck load I have had cattle for three different farmers living in three different

counties, and this has resulted in three different veterinarians having to make trips in order to read a truckload of twenty cattle. I suggest that this condition is not only costly but unnecessary. Then there is the inconvenience in getting cattle needled during the stocker season when every person buys them at the same time, and this results in costly delays that have a tendency to reduce buyers both for stocker and slaughter cattle.
If it were possible to move cattle in and out of these yards freely, there would be many occasions when the market is overloaded and shippers and farmers would take their cattle home, thereby stabilizing market conditions. If a farmer could remove his cattle from an overloaded market without being subject to the present regulations the expense would not be great, because trucks are always available at the first of the week for return loads. A clear stockyard would also result in providing an outlet for unfinished cattle that at times have a depressing effect on the prices received for all grades of cattle. Again, by removing obstacles that hinder movement in and out of the yards, farmers would be able to take this type of cattle away from the yards back to the farms for further feeding. It would provide a greater market for dairy type cattle for the same reason.
Perhaps the greatest financial gain that would result from declaring these yards an accredited area would be through a decrease in the number of cattle that are lost yearly from the disease that we farmers commonly call shipping fever. It is the fear of cattle coming in contact with this disease that makes farmers leery of leaving cattle in stockyards for the necessary three-day period of testing, or of holding them in some central place until they are read. I believe every feeder has benefited from the advances that have been made in the last four years in treating this costly disease. If a sick cattle beast is discovered in time, present treatment used by veterinarians is successful in nearly every case. However, under present conditions, if cattle are held for three days either in the stockyards or by a distributor, in too many cases by the time the farmer gets them on his own farm the disease is too far advanced to be successfully treated.
I understand that there are different types of serum now used in t.b. testing, and if cattle were injected with the proper type it would only mean holding them for one day at Winnipeg before shipping them into Ontario, or they could be injected at Winnipeg and read immediately on arrival in Ontario. I am sure that fair-minded stock

raisers in the western provinces realize the fairness of this proposal, because if an animal has t.b. and is loaded out for a point in Ontario it means that the whole load of cattle is exposed. The bringing of infected animals to Ontario also means added cost to the purchaser.
I feel this change in the present system of handling feeder cattle would mean dollars to both the seller and the buyer, because Ontario feeders will pay more, and can afford to pay more, if they know that they will not have to stand the loss on reactors, and if they can buy cattle and have them on their way home in an hour or so, thereby reducing to a large degree the risk of shipping fever.
I think the health of animals branch of the Department of Agriculture should be congratulated on the manner in which they handled the foot-and-mouth disease. I think the government deserves the thanks of all Canadians for the excellent application of support prices for livestock that prevailed during the last 18 months. When the embargo on Canadian exports of cattle and hogs to the United States was lifted last March, we found that in many cases our prices were higher than those being received by United States farmers. Support prices have been termed a joke by some hon. members in the house. I say they were no joke to the farmer with a stable full of cattle and hogs, and I feel sure that these same people would welcome any improvement in the present system that would mean a more efficient use of the veterinarian department by having a centralization of services at Winnipeg and Toronto which would be more economical to the taxpayers in general and beneficial to the Ontario buyers by reducing the time cattle are exposed to contagious diseases.

I should like to ask the minister whether he can give us any information with regard to the progress made, if any, by the committee on commodity problems set up under the food and agriculture organization. It was drawn to my attention the other day that when the hon. member for Melfort spoke last session, I believe it was, he stated in his speech that the minister had opposed the setting up of an international commodity clearing house. The minister interjected at that time and stated that while he knew that statement had been made it was not correct. As I happen to be one of the members who made that statement in the house, I should 68108-290

like to take this opportunity to justify what I have said on the matter.
I know very well that the minister has supported the general principle underlying an international commodity clearing house. The statement I made before was that when this matter was being discussed by the food and agriculture organization conference in 1949 and when a specific proposal was put forward by the food and agriculture organization council the minister stated at that time that he disagreed with the proposals contained in that proposition and therefore he was unable to support it. In order that there shall be no misunderstanding as to this matter, I should like to put on the record exactly what the minister stated, and then people who read the statement can judge whether or not I was correct in making the statement that I made.
This is at Washington?

It is the speech that the
minister made at Washington, and it is recorded in Foreign Trade. The minister said:
Canada, therefore, is prepared to give serious consideration to any international action designed to attain production and distribution of food. From this point of view, we are interested in the proposal advanced by the director general for an international commodity clearing house.
That is the statement on the point you raised.
Yes.
Canada is in favour of it.

Let me go on. The minister is in favour of the general principle, but he went on to say:
While endorsing the principle underlying this proposal, we are not in agreement with the means which, it has been suggested, are necessary to reach the objectives. In this connection, we may appear to agree with what has been said by the United Kingdom and United States representatives. Any transactions developed under the short term trading functions will be subject to concurrence by the governments concerned, and the major details of such transactions will also be subject to agreement by governments. This being the case, it hardly seems necessary to have an international agency actually buying and selling in commodity markets. It may even be questioned whether such activity in commodity markets by an international agency is desirable. It seems to us, therefore, that the question of the creation of a large capital fund for such a purpose is not necessarily an issue.
Lord Boyd Orr, in presenting his proposal for a world food board, had in mind the fact that the world had surpluses during certain periods and extreme shortages in other periods. It was his purpose to stabilize returns to producers and costs to consumers by setting aside surplus quantities in good years for periods of shortages. As has been pointed out in other conferences, however,

national governments can, and do, perform this function. We do not see that stocks held by an international agency will, in the short run, contribute to any improvement in the present situation. Canada, for example, has provided for the holding of stocks of wheat . . .
The minister points out that he supports the general principle, but on the other hand he disagrees with the means proposed.
No, no.

Let me quote it again. The minister said:
While endorsing the principle underlying this proposal, we are not in agreement with the means which, it has been suggested, are necessary to reach the objectives.
What I have actually said there is that the means that they suggested on that occasion were not what Sir John Boyd Orr was proposing at all.
Well, the point is that there was a specific proposal before the conference-
Right.

-for the setting up of an international commodity clearing house. When the vote was taken Canada opposed the setting up of that organization. I presume that was based on the minister's explanation for not being able to vote for the setting up of an international commodity clearing house at that time.
No, no; that was not an international commodity clearing house of the kind that Sir John had proposed at all.
Then the reason that the minister voted against it was a different reason from that stated in his speech.

No, no; I stated in my speech that my reason for voting against it was because of what Great Britain and the United States had said before I spoke, and what they actually did say was that they were not prepared to finance a scheme like Sir John's.
Therefore the minister voted against it because the United States and Great Britain were not in favour of it. That is an even worse reason.
We thought it would not work-and a lot of other people thought it would not work.

Let me read from the report of the conference which gave the reasons for its being turned down:
(a) That the accumulation of inconvertible currency would represent additional indebtedness by the deficit countries involving the burden of eventual repayment in terms of additional exports of goods and services and would have the effect of delaying the general convertibility.

That is clause (a). Clause (d) reads:
(d) That the financial functions proposed for the ICCH could be performed by the governments directly involved.
That is the reason I gave when I spoke in the house.

I explained it to you at that time but you did not accept my explanation then, and apparently you are not accepting it now; nevertheless it is correct. Why not go back and look up all of the other conferences at which the same question was discussed? It was discussed at every FAO meeting that was held; and I made a speech at every one of those meetings supporting Lord Boyd Orr, and I made another one in Rome supporting Lord Orr's proposal.

I am not interested in the various speeches but I am interested in the action that was taken by Canada in reference to the specific proposal for setting up an international commodity clearing house. That was the proposal before the conference and Canada voted against it. The minister can give his own reasons-I thought the speech probably gave the reasons why Canada opposed it inasmuch as the speech was made at the time.
The report of the conference gives the reasons why the conference opposed the proposal. I suppose those reasons will include the reasons why Canada opposed it. The interesting point, and the point I made, was that when the specific proposal was placed before the FAO conference in December, 1949, Canada voted against it. That is the point I am interested in.
The statement which my hon. friend makes when he is out in the country and which he thinks he is making now are the same-
Exactly the same.

They may be exactly the same but that is not the interpretation that anyone puts on them. The suggestion made by the speaker-the suggestion that was made the other day when I referred to it-is that I was not in support of Lord Orr's proposal for an international organization to handle certain agricultural products. The member goes on to say that he knows I was not in favour of it because I voted against it in Washington. That is not true-and the statement does not say it is true either. The statement actually shows that this was not a proposal such as Lord Orr discussed with the FAO conference. He had been refused support by Britain and by the United States. Their reasons were that, quite naturally from their point of view, they were not going to

become involved in financing all the rest of the world's surpluses and thought they should not do so. If they are not going to be in it there are no other countries in the world that can do the job.
If my hon. friend reads my speech over he will find that I said there, as elsewhere, that I could not understand why countries like the United States and Britain could not do a thing of that kind because 250,000 farmers in western Canada carried 600 million bushels of wheat from the middle of the war until the end of the war in order to save those very people from starvation. I said that the government of Canada did not help them do that, nor did the governments of Britain and the United States. Those farmers carried that wheat and paid all the costs of carrying it from 1941 to the end of the war in order to have it available at the end of the war to help feed people who would otherwise have starved.
I have said at every one of the meetings that since 250,000 farmers could do that job, which was the job Lord Orr was saying ought to be done with regard to wheat, coffee, wool and other non-perishable products, I could not see any reason why two great financial powers could not find some way of backing Lord Orr's program. That is the position I have always taken.
At the meeting in Washington, Britain and the United States took the same position that they have always taken, that they were not going to finance any scheme such as this proposal involved. It was pretty obvious that the next country in line was Canada and that we were being asked to do some financing that we did not believe we were capable of doing. If we went into a scheme of that kind with a group of nations that would not accept the principles that were laid down by Lord Orr, then of course we would be looking for trouble; so we voted against it. We did not vote against any international project set up on the basis of Lord Orr's ideas, and Lord Orr himself would not have said that the other proposals were in line with his ideas. We said that we could not go along with the scheme and that was all that was said. I have never at any time opposed Lord Orr's scheme and at every meeting it has been brought up.

Any time that I have spoken on this question in the country I have made it very, very clear just what proposal I was referring to. I pointed out that this was a matter in which the federation of agriculture had shown a great deal of interest in the past. It is a question in which a lot of interest has been taken by the international 68108-290J

Mr. Chairman, before the committee rose for the luncheon recess, the discussion on this item had ranged over a wide field. I wish to participate in the debate and to bring to the attention of the committee some of the problems which are perplexing agriculture in the constituency which I have the honour to represent.
The constituency of Perth lies in a great fertile area in western Ontario. It is a great mixed farming section. Our county produces large numbers of bacon hogs, great quantities of butter and concentrated milk, and the northern section of the constituency is renowned for its production of cheese.
The problem of imitation dairy products is arousing much concern among producers of all types of dairy products. They realize that if the extension of the use of synthetics becomes more widespread, great harm will be wrought upon the whole dairy industry. The dairy industry has been responsible for a great measure of the prosperity which has been enjoyed by the farmers of western Ontario. It has contributed to a great extent to the conservation of the soil and it fits in admirably with a program for better land use.

Supply-Agriculture
Some years ago there was distributed a bulletin-I am not sure whether it was distributed by the federal Department of Agriculture or the department of agriculture of the province of Ontario-entitled "The Cow, The Mother of Prosperity". That bulletin contained some extremely valuable information. I regret that the copy I had has since passed out of my hands. It seems to me that it would be quite appropriate to make a speech on that subject, but I do not intend to attempt to do so at this busy time. However, I am convinced that a great many of the people of Canada are not aware of that fact and of the great importance of the dairy industry.
Compared with the price of many foods and many luxuries, the price of dairy products in the past few years has been low. Many dairy farmers have depended upon the sale of surplus breeding stock in order to augment the income received from the sale of dairy products. In the last year there has been a marked decline in the price received for dairy cattle, and the returns of the dairy-farmers have been considerably lower because of that fact. The imposition of the United States embargo a little bit over a year ago prevented the export of a large number of dairy cattle which had been raised for that purpose. When the border was reopened on March 1 of this year, prices in the United States had declined and producers are now obliged to take prices which are at least 30 per cent lower than they were a year and a half ago. The high price of beef had a supporting effect upon the price of dairy cattle, and the decline in beef prices has also contributed to a lower income for the dairy farmer.
Producers of milk for concentrated milk products and butter are fortunate that they are protected against any drastic further reduction in the price of their products because of the action of the government in agreeing to purchase butter at 58 cents a pound for two years and the decision to buy ten million pounds of concentrated milk powder.
The cheese producer has no such assurance. It is believed that there will be an increase in cheese production this year. As I pointed out earlier, the closing of the United States market compelled many farmers to retain more livestock on their farms. Many of these cattle will be in production this year; and if weather conditions are favourable, everything points to a great increase in the amount of milk offered the various markets.
With no market available, except the domestic one, manufacturers of processed cheese may be in a position to secure their requirements at much lower prices than those prevailing a year ago. In other words, it looks

like a buyers' market. We are informed that there is a small surplus of 1952 cheese in the hands of the trade; I am told that it is no larger than it was a year ago. It is fortunate that the arrangements were made to export cheese to the United Kingdom. We only wish that the British had more dollars with which to buy more.
Another feature of the present situation which I ought to draw to the attention of the committee is the fact that an attractive price for butter may divert large quantities of milk from the manufacture of cheese to butter. The result might easily be a surplus of butter in the hands of the government; and that surplus might be extremely difficult to dispose of. Apparently butter is not in demand elsewhere in the world. There is no doubt that, should any surplus occur, cheese could be disposed of.
I would suggest that the government, through the agricultural prices support board, give some consideration to purchasing cheese in a manner similar to that in which butter is being so efficiently handled. The government has decided to continue the purchase of butter at 58 cents per pound for a period of two years and in addition, as I said before, has offered to purchase ten million pounds of milk powder. This action has been hailed with approval by producer organizations and removes some of the uncertainty surrounding their operations. If similar assurance were given the producers of cheese, a price of 30 cents per pound would be comparable.
I would also suggest that the cheese producers marketing board-and I speak of the cheese producers marketing board of Ontario -devote a great deal more attention to the problem of marketing cheese in Canada. There are a few commercial organizations which are making a strong effort to market natural cheddar cheese, but a number of the larger buyers are much more interested in the processing and sale of special cheeses made from cheddar cheese and other materials. What the cheese industry needs is more consumers. A little bit over a year ago I suggested in this chamber that if everyone in Canada would consume another half pound of cheese, the surplus would vanish. I should like to repeat the suggestion today, but in view of larger production, I should like to raise that amount to one pound.

I had not intended to take part in this debate. Owing to some of the things that the minister said this morning in answer to the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, perhaps I should say something. I have enjoyed listening to some of the representations made by my neighbour members,

and I just wish to say that I agree wholeheartedly with most of the things they said, with the exception of the praise that they heaped on the government, praise which I do not think they should have given. Be that as it may, I still agree with many of the things they said. The hon. member for Wellington North gave the minister a few ideas that were commendable, and I think he should pay attention to them.
The hon. member for Grey North said at page 4567 of Hansard:
They have confidence in this government, but this combination of falling beef prices and rising costs has them worried.
I hope they have confidence in the government; I cannot say that I have. We will all find out sooner or later just how much confidence they have in the government, and until that time comes I shall be satisfied to wait and find out.
When the minister was answering the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton with respect to the number of hogs in that province he gave the number as of last June. The number that was given as of that particular date would have nothing to do with the number that is there now. I would suggest that the minister get up to date on his figures, because I know as well as the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton that the hog population has decreased considerably, and has decreased very rapidly from October 1 to January 1 owing to the policy of the government.
They announced three months ahead that 3 cents was coming off the floor price. The result was that a lot of brood sows were marketed that should never have been sold. After the price was lowered to 23 cents the market took care of it from there on, and inside of two months the price had risen not only to 26 cents but had gone above that, and is now 28 cents or 29 cents per pound. Because of that we have not nearly as many hogs as we should have, and we have a larger number than we had two months ago. Hogs are a line that increase very rapidly and diminish just as quickly. If it had not been for the policy of the Minister of Agriculture and of the government, of lowering the floor under hogs by 3 cents, we would not be in the position that we were in, in January and February, where the packers could not find enough hogs to process.
I do not know whether the condition has improved a great deal since then or not; but one thing is sure. We are not overpopulated in hogs at the present time. That policy may have been created by the minister intentionally because we had a surplus of

pork and he did not want a surplus of hogs at this particular time. When the minister has an idea like that he should tell it to the producer and not leave him to guess and flounder around and not know what he is doing.
I spoke about the floor price under beef. Well, I happen to be a beef producer myself, and like a good many more I have taken quite a loss on beef. We all took a 10-cent drop when the embargo was put on beef going across to the United States. It was a decided 10-cent drop right on the face of it. I am not particularly sympathetic to those of us who had been in the business for some time and had had a chance to make some money two or three years previously, but I was alarmed about the young farmer who was starting up and who had put all he had into cattle and then found himself in the position where it was absolutely impossible for him to pay the bank. As you know, the bank will carry you only so long as they can see a way clear to get their money back. These boys lost a great deal of money, and some of them will never be able to farm again. I felt sorry for these boys, because some of them were returned men and deserved a better fate than that. I do not know that that was the minister's fault. I am not blaming him for the foot-and-mouth epidemic in Canada, which had a lot to do with it.
Then the market in the United States fell rapidly from that day until the embargo was lifted, and our price was higher than theirs, and up to the moment the lifting of the embargo has not done us very much good, apart from the fact that it has given a chance to the dairymen to sell surplus breeding stock, cows and breeding stock of that kind, to the United States. Quite a number of dairy cattle are going across the line, and that will eliminate a certain number of dairy cattle that otherwise would have gone onto our market. For that reason it may be a help.
In regard to beef prices, a little more attention should have been paid to the amount of money that was charged for beef on the block as well as the price that the farmer was getting. The butchers were charging too much for the cuts that they sold over the counter at a time when they were able to buy cows for 12 cents and 15 cents a pound. The floor price of beef was 26 cents, but it did not work out as a floor so much as a ceiling so far as the packers were concerned. They were in a position where they did not have to pay more than 26 cents, because that was the floor, and they did not pay more than 26 cents except on two or three occasions when

Supply-Agriculture
the market was slim. They paid 27 cents on one or two occasions, when not enough stock came on the market to keep the plants open, and they had to pay a little more. Because of that fact they did not have to go over 26 cents. Twenty-six cents was the top.
The 26-cent floor applied only to one grade of beef, and had nothing to do with butcher heifers and cows. As I said before, they were selling as low as 12 cents and 15 cents. Quite a few of them were going over the block and were being sold as choice beef. They are choice beef; if they are properly fed and fed quickly they are just as good as younger beef. The fact remains that the butchers and the packers made a lot more money out of the regulations with respect to the price of beef than did the farmers. The farmers lost money and the packers reaped the benefit.
Something should have been done to see that the farmers were not blamed for the high cost of beef that was being sold over the counter. There are several other things I want to say. I wanted to speak about the dairy business for a little while. We have lost practically all of our dairy market. We have lost the United Kingdom market. I do not think that is to the credit of this government. Perhaps they could not do anything else; perhaps they felt they could not do anything else. They could have done something else. They could have made dollars available to Britain.
I think Great Britain would have bought a lot of our dairy products if they had had any money with which to buy them. I think we can blame this government in that regard because it has not had a policy which would allow Britain to have dollars with which to buy those products. The United States was a good market, so long as we had it. But just as soon as they reach the position where they do not want our products, due to their growing the same kind of products as are grown in this country, they say they have no further need for what we produce, and we have to look elsewhere.
I hope the government will look into the markets of the world with a view to finding us a better market for our dairy products. For some years we have had no market for our cheese, with the result that we have a large supply on hand-the very best cheese to be found. This, again, has caused a great deal of worry to our dairy farmers.
I was pleased by the suggestion made some time ago by three counties that said they were going to pool their milk supplies. I made that suggestion on one occasion in the house a few years ago, and am convinced it

is the only solution to the problem. If I live on one side of a road and sell my milk to a dairy, and my neighbour lives on the other side and sells his milk to an evaporated milk processing plant, and there is considerable difference in the price, I do not think that is right. I believe milk should be sold by grade; regardless of the market it finds it should bring the same price, established according to quality.
I intend to make some further observations when the separate items are called, and shall defer until that time anything further I wish to say.

That is only your opinion.

Possibilities in the proposed chemical industry in Canada, expected to follow in the wake of oil and natural gas resources development in western Canada, opens the door for increased markets of inedible fats of agricultural origin, of which we have an accumulating surplus in Canada. Since the war, consumption of inedible animal fats has not kept pace with the increased supply, even at present depressed prices. Today, new chemicals known in other countries offer possibilities for greatly expanded use of inedible fats, such as tallow and grease. From chemical derivatives of pork grease it is possible to make a wide variety of products, including lubricants, insecticides, and various surface coatings for oilcloth and plastic coated materials. These possibilities appear to be advisable alternatives to uneconomic palliatives which serve only to prolong the problem, and for a time ease or postpone the penalties.
I suggest that this government, not only through the Department of Agriculture but the Department of Finance, should recognize the necessity of research in the field of agriculture because it has paid off in other fields. When I first spoke 1 mentioned research in the forest industry where today by-products which formerly were simply considered waste material now form a large part of their revenue. If that same principle were applied to agriculture I think the people of this country would benefit greatly. I do not think there would be any opposition from any hon. member to the adoption by the government of ways and means to ensure that those engaged in agriculture will intensify their effort so that not only will they be benefited, but there will be benefit for the whole economy of Canada.

There is one important point I should like to stress and that is the greater use of agricultural products. In the United States, where much more research into the use of agricultural products in industry has been undertaken than in Canada, in 1951 $1,250 million worth of farm raw materials were purchased by industry. In other words, the relatively new industrial uses for agricultural products in the United States contributed over $1,250 million of profitable outlet for agricultural production which otherwise would have been surplus. A new market worth $1,250 million did not completely solve the problem of surpluses in the United States but it proved most convincingly that the use of new products offers a sound approach to this problem.
The developments in the field of scientific agriculture have of necessity been retarded during the past decade because of the interest in and the urgency of scientific advances in the field of defence, necessitated by all-out war and war preparedness programs. As a result the advances in scientific agriculture in the past decade or two have been comparatively small in. comparison with the progress made at other times in this field. The number of new products is an example of this fact. Our economy at the present time is threatened by a surplus production of many products when those products are considered in the light of their utility value for food alone. I am confident, however, that with adequate scientific research in the direction of greater utilization of some of those products in the industrial field, surpluses and threatened surpluses would not plague the Canadian producer.
It is particularly important at this time that leadership in the field of agricultural research, designed to bring about greater utilization of the productive capacity of agriculture and towards supplying the ever-increasing demands for raw materials by industry, should be undertaken at top government levels. It is quite true that a certain amount of research is done by the federal and provincial governments, and a liberal amount by private industry; but if the potential agricultural possibilities of Canada are to be utilized as a source of greater raw materials for industry, then I think the government should take the initial action in this field and provide adequate money for continuing research along the lines suggested.
This nation today is going through a transition from an agrarian to an industrial economy. In the wake of this development there has been created, and is being created every day, an ever-increasing demand for raw materials. Many of these, even of a very 68108-291
Supply-A griculture
primary nature, which are being imported into this country at the present time, could and should be produced on the farms of Canada. Soybean oil is an example.
One other aspect towards which leadership in research should be directed is the greater utilization of waste materials and by-products possible from this source of supply. Sugar beets are an illustration, the pectin from sugar beets, and also the pectin from apples. The possibilities in this field have hardly been scratched.
I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that the very creditable record of the national farm chemurgic council in the United States warrants serious consideration by his department of the possibilities for greater utilization of the products of agriculture in this country, many of which are either entirely unused or wasted as by-products, and which many times even constitute a problem as to disposal.

There was no objection taken by the one occupying the chair at that time or by any member of the opposition. It was a well-prepared speech. Who prepared it I do not know, but it was

listened to with a great deal of interest. I make no criticism of that hon. member for having read his speech because it was one which was welcomed by every member of the house. The speech I happen to be making is of a technical nature.
