speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I should like that to be made clear.

There is no such thought in my mind and I do not wish to imply that. I simply repeat that I have been a member for several years and have listened to speeches of different kinds being read, including technical speeches like the one to which I have referred and which was welcomed by the house the other day. Such speeches certainly require a series of notes to guide one in making one's presentation. My speech at this time deals with research and is not an easy one to make. I know that it has taken hours and hours to prepare. I do not like to place on the record something that is not factual and which the government would not consider having their officials study with some interest. I only have a few more words to put on the record. I think I have been fair in my reference to a government spokesman. It was something that we in our party welcomed. I do not say that the speech made by Dr. Firestone was made by a government spokesman, but I think I share the opinion held from coast to coast that his speech and the speech made the other day in New York along the same lines by Dr. Hall, the president of Western Ontario university, are speeches that are welcome irrespective of whether you are in the government or in the opposition, in public life or a private citizen and they dealt with this same subject. These speeches are welcomed because they contain material that I think we all appreciate having the opportunity to digest.
As I said at the start, I think that every member of the house regardless of party welcomes a greater effort by this government or any government at other levels to make a further contribution to the agricultural economy of the country if it can be done through more research along that line. I would also suggest, as I did earlier, that the Minister of Finance as well as the Minister of Agriculture give consideration to the possibilities for the development of this country by greater encouragement to research by private enterprise. They too can work in co-operation with the

various levels of government and the other agencies engaged in research to which I referred earlier in my speech. I think that the Minister of Finance and the government should consider our taxation laws in the light of the great potential that lies ahead for this nation if we undertake the research necessary for that great development.

Mr. Chairman, there is one matter I want to take up with the minister for the purpose of securing his views thereon. Mention has been made on a number of occasions of the attitude taken by the United States of America in imposing import bans on Canadian agricultural products, dairy products and certain oils which are products of agriculture. Reference has also been made to the discussion that took place recently in the United States as a result of which President Eisenhower requested those in charge of the commission having to do with the question of the importation of agricultural products to also impose a ban upon the importation of feed oats into the United States.
However, I refer particularly to dairy products. I should like the minister to give the house and the country more information than was furnished to the house recently by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce in response to questions as to what positive action the Canadian government intends to take for the purpose of bringing to the attention of the government of the United States in the firmest manner possible the grave injustice already done to Canadian agriculture by the actions taken thus far by the United States and also the injustice that will be done by the contemplated action recently revealed.
Only recently the dairymen of Canada met in the city of Edmonton and there was considerable discussion on this subject, one that affects the farm prosperity in this country to a degree that few realize. At the meeting of the national dairy council in Edmonton in convention one of the main subjects of discussion was the warning that the United States might dump huge surpluses of dairy products on world markets and that Canadian industry would be seriously threatened. The president of the organization, Mr. J. J. Creighton, made this statement among others to the delegates:
Canadian dairymen have a real and justified fear that the American government will dump its enormous stockpile of dairy products on markets throughout the world at fire-sale prices.
This has been done before and a repetition would be grossly unfair, not only to Canada but to other surplus-producing countries-
I feel that it is a matter which falls particularly within the ambit of the Minister

of Agriculture and one that deserves a statement on his part. It is one that must exercise not only his mind but the minds of the officials of his department. It is challenging in its prospect and dangerous to the maintenance of Canada's productive agricultural dairy machine, if I might use that term.
What means of co-operation are followed between Canada and the United States now that we are joining together in a common effort for the preservation of freedom? What arrangements are there so that nations within NATO will not, by their own nationalistic actions, endanger the agricultural survival of any one of the members of NATO? That is the first matter I bring to the minister's attention. Up to the present time all that we in the house know is that two notes have been sent to the government of the United States of America. On one occasion when the matter arose I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether any replies to those notes had been received. The implication in his remarks in response to my question was that no answer was sought or inferred in the notes that were sent.
I think that the strongest possible protest ought to be made against these bans; because, if this attitude continues, we will go back to the conditions of the 1920's when the Fordney-McCumber tariff-engendered or conceived as a result of strong agrarian appeals in various parts of the United States -and the Hawley-Smoot tariff were brought into being. Our memories recall the very damaging effect that those tariffs had on our agricultural economy. My remarks apply particularly to eastern Canada, the maritimes and British Columbia, and certainly the action taken recently by the United States has not been conducive to that attitude of co-operation which should be the concept of nations joined together in a common dedication to freedom. I would like to hear from the minister too about the degree to which Canada within the last few months-since January of 1953-has been importing agricultural products from the United States. What has been the extent of the importation of bacon and other farm products from the United States during the period I have mentioned? It seems passing strange that the situation prevails that imports should be taking place, having particular regard to the fact that surpluses are beginning to pile up or have already piled up.
Then I wish also to suggest that when representations are made to the United States of America it might be pointed out, having regard to our surplus of agricultural products or anticipated surpluses, that if no quotas and no embargoes were placed against them at all 68108-291J
Supply-Agriculture
they would only have a 2 per cent impact on the farm economy of the United States.
The United States may have been able to justify nationalistic actions such as embargoes and the like against Canadian farm products thirty years ago. At that time the United States had accepted no world responsibilities and had no world responsibilities to discharge. Now, however, we are all in the same boat. One of the most serious things that could happen to Canada would be that, as a result of actions such as I have indicated, our agricultural productive capacity would not be expanded. Then we would not be able to discharge our responsibility of producing agricultural products to meet ever-increasing world demand-an endeavour for which we are fitted.
I realize, as far as our agricultural production is concerned, that, as years go by and our population increases, naturally more and more of our Canadian farm production will be absorbed by our home market. Until we have achieved that population we, with our vast agricultural acreage, must necessarily continue to increase our production. Certainly everything possible should be done by the government to bring to the attention of the government of the United States the very definite need of co-operation, and a very definite condemnation of action that can but have a tremendously detrimental effect on our agricultural economy.
That is particularly so when the United States is in a position where it takes delivery of such a large proportion of our mineral and our strategic metal production. Those things it needs, and it is taking them; but at the same time, to the degree that has been achieved already and which may well be extended by the further action referred to during the last few days in the United States House of Representatives, the United States is extending or expanding this field of closed markets to Canada. It applies in connection with other natural products. It applies in connection with fish. Those are things which I believe deserve the serious consideration of parliament and deserve on the part of the government assurance from members in all parts of the chamber that, in any stand taken by the government to bring this matter to the attention of the United States government, the minister or the government may be assured that he or they speak with the authority of members from all parts of this country and from all parts of the chamber.
There is one other matter to which I should like to refer while I am on my feet. I do not like to rise every few moments in order to deal with other matters. I am diffi-

Supply-A griculture
dent about bringing this matter to the attention of the minister because it might naturally be said to me, "After all, you are not a farmer". On a number of occasions in the United States, within the last year or so, in restaurants and in hotels I have seen references to the fact that served on the menu was Canadian bacon. In reality it is not Canadian bacon at all. It is United States bacon with the fat portion removed. I have spoken to a number of Americans in this regard and they have assured me that there is an obvious demand in the United States for what is known as Canadian bacon, namely lean bacon, different in kind and quality from United States bacon. I have also been informed that United States packers are most anxious to supply the demand and that they would generally be prepared to pay a premium in order to get Canadian bacon.
One organization that was in touch with me through its representative-he was a representative of an agricultural group influential in this country-advised me that it was their considered opinion that the United States public would be prepared to pay up to 5 cents per pound premium if it could get Canadian bacon. The situation at the present time is that the demand for the type of bacon to which I have made reference is not being met. I would ask the minister what has been done along this line, towards creating a demand in the United States and a supply on the part of Canada to the United States, to meet a situation which, if my information is correct-and certainly my informants are reliable and also knowledgeable persons-would have a pronounced effect in extending the demand for Canadian bacon and also in maintaining prices for the Canadian farmers.
Having made those few remarks, I would greatly appreciate it if the minister would be prepared to discuss them, with particular reference to the first matter to which I have directed his attention. There is in Canada today, in every province, a strong body of opinion that greatly resents the attitude now being taken and the further attitude that is expected to be taken, which will have but one effect, and that a most detrimental one, on the Canadian agricultural industry.

With regard to the last matter that was spoken of, namely the matter of marketing bacon in the United States, may I say that I have seen the menus in the United States mentioning Canadian bacon. Sometimes the menu mentions Canadian style of bacon. It does not always say it is Canadian bacon. Canadian style of bacon is the lean bacon.
That is right.

Even if it is United States bacon, it may have some of the fat trimmed off-and it is back bacon probably-and be called Canadian style. Nevertheless, before the foot-and-mouth disease epidemic, there was quite an effort being made to have long, lean Canadian hogs introduced into the United States market. We were being fairly successful in some directions in that regard. Since the embargo has gone off, of course that effort is being continued and there is a gradual increase in the amount; but it has not yet reached any great proportions since the embargo.
As to the other question having to do with dairy products entering the United States, as was indicated by him, the hon. member for Lake Centre received his answers, to the questions he asked in the house, from the Minister of Trade and Commerce, from the Prime Minister and to an extent from the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he has been here. It is natural that that is where the answers should come from.
I do not think I should attempt to say anything which is in any sense different from what has already been said. After all, those ministers naturally speak with regard to government policy on matters having to do with trade. As Minister of Agriculture I am interested in products that concern farmers' returns. But we have a man in Washington by the name of Mr. Hopper who is associated with the Department of Trade and Commerce as agricultural representative. He is there continuously. We have almost daily contacts with him through the Department of Trade and Commerce. AH these questions related to dairy products and that sort of thing are matters he is discussing with the department down there almost daily. Any representations we have to make to the United States department are naturally made to our representative and are made direct. We get answers back from time to time with regard to what the attitudes are.
I just repeat that in order to show that that is the method by which most of the representation is made. We do not get into a discussion which gets onto the front pages of the paipetr and says, "We do not agree with what the Americans are doing". After all, the greater part of trade in food that goes on between the two countries is controlled, in so far as duties are concerned, by the agreements that were entered into back in 1947 and again in 1950. Those agreements were international. They resulted in considerable reductions in duties, approximately 50 per cent on a great many commodities.
[Mr. Diefenbaker.1

Of course it is true that recently the United States government has undertaken to apply embargoes on certain products, a fact which means that it does not matter a great deal what the duty is; the product is not allowed to be imported for the time being and therefore we have no trade in it. All we can do is to make protests-and we do so-and then present our point of view to them. That is the job of these men we have down there. They keep constant pressure on in order to try to get the matter changed back to where it was. We are successful from time to time in getting certain things done; but we cannot always accomplish what we think ought to be accomplished. I sometimes become a little bit impatient with our own people-with our farm organizations, for example-in that some of the things that I think are more important than are many of the things that are talked about are never mentioned at all.
Mention has been made of oats and barley. Agriculture must see to it that enough oats and barley stays in this country to take care of our livestock industry. I am not going to worry too much about our having an extra supply of oats. We have an extra supply of oats now. We have had an extra heavy crop of oats for three years in a row; but from farming experience I learned long ago not to sell any oats from my farm. I have more oats on my farm right now than I have ever had at any time in my experience, but I am not selling any oats. I have enough cattle and hogs to eat all the oats I grow on an average over any five-year period, and I know from experience that one of these years I am not going to grow very many oats, and most people in western Canada know that. Therefore just to take the figures of all the oats that there are in western Canada does not mean a great deal. If we are in a good position, if we have more oats than we are going to feed in the next year, it is because we may need them the year following, and farmers do maintain more oats than they need at the moment.
The other matter is that there is a straight embargo against the importation of wheat into the United States. I find it almost impossible to get anybody to pay any attention to that. It is the most serious problem from the point of view of the western wheat growers that there is in the world situation today. It has been so all the time. The question of what we are going to do with our wheat would not be nearly so difficult if it were not that there is an embargo against shipping wheat into the United States. That in itself increases acreage in the United States from 62 million up to 83 million acres, and when you get 25 million acres, which is equal to
Supply-Agriculture
our own acreage, of extra wheat in the United States it certainly has a bearing on the whole world situation. But we do not say much about that. We talk a lot about some things that are much smaller, and we do not say much about that. I must say that every time I go down to Washington and every time I meet anybody from there I spend more time talking about that than I do about some of the other things that are referred to. The dairy end of it is most important, particularly when we have considerable surpluses to export. But we always have surpluses of the other products to export in great quantity, and that situation is important to us.
Therefore I would answer the question by saying that we keep the pressure on all the time through the set-up that we have, the relationships we have created between this country and the United States, in dealing with any obstruction to trade that may exist between the two countries in an endeavour to get them removed as much as possible. All I can say at the moment is that they are removed at this time to as large an extent as they have ever been over a very long period of time.
Would the minister also at this time give the information I asked for as to the importations of farm products into Canada?

I do not think I have the figures here. They may be here if I looked through my records. A year ago I was down to Chicago and Milwaukee on a sort of speaking trip, and I did have occasion at that time to look into these figures. I was surprised to find that the trade in farm products is equally divided between the two countries. My memory is that there is only a difference of a few million dollars between the amount that we ship to the United States and the amount that the United States ships here. One might be surprised at that but we do bring into this country a considerable quantity of citrus fruits. My memory is that it runs to about $50 million. We do import from the United States a considerable amount of cotton, which is a farm product. It runs to about another $50 million. And in spite of the little discussion we had here the other day, we do import a considerable quantity of potatoes.
And cheese.

These potatoes are imported into this country at a season of the year when new potatoes are not available here. The new potatoes we eat in the restaurants now are, I presume, United States potatoes. For a period of the year we get a considerable quantity, but when you balance it all up, my

Supply-Agriculture
memory is that-I do not just have the figures in my mind at the moment-at that time the figures were about $250 million going from one country to the other in products of different kinds, including all of our grains and everything of that kind.
It is important that that trade should continue. I think everyone considers it is important that it should continue. There is one thing about it which strikes me as important. One hundred and fifty million people on the other side of the line consume our food products, whatever they are, but we have not so many on this side. If we are consuming almost as much with our smaller population, we are consuming much more per head of population than they are on the other side of the line.

Of course citrus foods and the like are agricultural products, but what I want the minister to do is to provide the committee with the total imports to date from the United States into Canada of bacon, eggs, cheese and farm products of that kind in the years 1952 and 1953. These food products are not seasonal, and they are indigenous to our agricultural economy. These are the figures I want. I realize that there is almost equality as between the exports of agricultural products from Canada to the United States and the imports in return. Certainly there is no great competition in the imports of citrus fruits into Canada and the like, or the fruits in season.
What I have in mind in particular is this. In 1952 and 1953 surpluses of agricultural products were commencing to pile up in this country. It is a strange fact that at a time like this we should be importing agricultural products which we have in excess in Canada. In addition to the minister furnishing particulars of bacon, eggs, cheese and the like, all farm products, that have come from the	United	States into Canada	in 1952and 1953	up to	date, I also	wish	him to
provide the committee with imports of cheese and other farm products from the commonwealth countries as well.

If I search through my records I	think	I shall find	these	figureshere, and	I will do that when	we get down
to the different items.
As long as the minister will do that, that is all right.
As I see it now, I do not think 1952 would be a very good year to take. That is the year in which we had the foot-and-mouth disease and had an embargo on most shipments.

If the minister will take
1951	I will not argue with him. Take 1951,
1952	and 1953 to date.
Yes, we will get those figures. It might be well to put 1952 by itself and get another three-year period, the one preceding it, because 1952 is so unusual on account of foot-and-mouth disease.

I want to refer to a point made by the hon. member for Lake Centre which seems to me to be a very important one. I do it partly because the Secretary of State for External Affairs is in his seat at the moment. The hon. member for Lake Centre pointed out the fact that we are still engaged in a great common military enterprise, although it is not at the stage of actual war. He pointed out that when we were at the stage of war it was felt that military and economic co-operation were virtually of equal importance. At that time we made tremendous adjustments so that economic strength and military strength could march hand in hand.
The minister has pointed out-and I accept his answer-that part of the question asked by the hon. member for Lake Centre, namely the diplomatic representations and representations from the Department of Trade and Commerce, should be answered by the ministers responsible for that; but it does seem to me that the point which the hon. member has raised is one of far-reaching importance. At the present time when there do seem to be strong indications that the United States, in spite of expectations which I at any rate entertained to the contrary, are forgetting that. It seems to me that the point is one which the government should keep very much in its mind. It is fortunate that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who for many months has been engaged in what might be called a common task, will now have more time for the affairs of our own country. Certainly there is enough happening at the present time to disturb us greatly.
Some five years ago I met a distinguished American statesman who was frank in saying that just as soon as there were American surpluses of farm products we might, unfortunately, return to the era we knew so well in the twenties and the thirties.
Then, one other thing. The minister said -and I was surprised by what he said; I do not think I misunderstood him-some things about an embargo on export wheat, and then he proceeded to say, "I find it almost impossible to get anyone to take an interest in it." Was he referring to the United States or Canada?
I said that farm organizations do not talk about that very much in their meetings. I do not find them talking about it at all. Other members might; but that is not what I find.
Will the minister furnish later on the information for which I have asked, before the estimates are finally passed?
When we come to the livestock and dairy items.

Then I have a further question in connection with expenditures being made in connection with feed grain subsidies which, I believe, come under the minister's department. What is the situation in that matter; and is it a fact that those who are entitled to these subsidies have not been receiving them during the last several months? And if so, why have not those payments been made?

There was a short period of time before the first of April when we ran out of funds, because our vote of last year was not quite large enough. But as soon as we got the funds the payments were made- since April 1.
For how long did that condition continue?
For about six weeks. We ran out of money about six weeks before the end of the fiscal year, and we had to explain to those people that the payments would be made as soon as we received the funds.

Item agreed to.
Science service-
6.	Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, $1,534,850.

I do not know whether my question can properly be asked under item 5 or item 6, but in the details respecting operation and maintenance it is indicated that co-operative investigations have been carried on, for which the sum of $110,350 is required. Would the minister give the committee some details concerning those investigations, and what the results have been.

I shall do that; but just while we are looking up the information on that item I should like to say something which has been impressed upon me ever since this sound system has been in use in this chamber. I have been sitting here a long time, and I used to think it would be better if we had a sound system. But I would like to say to those in the gallery directing it that I have never found it more difficult to hear what is going on in the house than I have since this sound system has been put in.
The point is this, that before the sound system was put in, when anyone rose in his place in any part of the house I knew where the sound was coming from. Now, however, I have to look all over the house
Supply-Agriculture
to find out who is rising to his feet. And, to start with, I find that a most difficult situation. Then I find that sometimes the sound is blasting right at me through the device on my desk, while at other times it does not seem to get to me at all. I am saying this because I find that difficulty, and indeed I found it only a moment ago in connection with what was said. I would hope that some way might be found of directing it a little better than it has been directed, if that is possible. And, if not, I am afraid I may have to start making the same kind of objections that others were making before, because they could not hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Do you want television with it, too?

While the minister is looking up the information in reply to the hon. member for Melfort, I should like to ask questions connected with items Nos. 6, 9, 12 and 14, because they all have to do with land and equipment. I notice that under science service there is an amount of $2,053,020 for those four items. Would the minister give us some details?
Then, turning to the item for experimental farms, we find votes of the same kind which total $1,103,000. Perhaps the minister would give the information at one time. And I might say, while the information is being prepared-
Well, perhaps we should clear up one thing at a time.
There is no information in the explanatory notes to say what these expenditures are for.
Dealing first with the question asked by the hon. member for Melfort, I wonder if he would give some indication of where the items to which he referred are located.
I was referring to page 82, where the minister will see about half-way down the page reference to co-operative investigations.
That is in connection with ordinary grants to universities in connection with co-operative arrangements we have with them and with others for these investigations.
Do the universities receive the grants?

Yes, right across the country, wherever agricultural colleges are associated with universities, and research work is being done. We have arrangements to make grants to them, and those grants require this amount of money.

Supply-Agriculture
Is there any list showing the amounts granted to each university?
Yes, there is a list. We can get it.
I would like to have it on the record.

In connection with this item of $110,350 for co-operative investigations I would say that there is a reduction in the amount. This item provides funds for the continuation of co-operative research projects initiated in 1951-52 and 1952-53, and for important new projects to be undertaken in 1953-54. The chief aim of these grants is to obtain scientific information and data on specific projects which it is not possible to obtain as economically, or for reasons of lack of facilities or suitable trained staff in the various laboratories of the service.
The co-operators in connection with most of these projects are outstanding authorities in various scientific fields, who are to be found on the staffs of Canadian universities. It is

How much has been spent on the science building at Sault Ste. Marie? If possible I would like the figures as to the building and then as to the apparatus or mechanical equipment.

There is about $50,000 voted this year and I think there will be about $60,000 more before it can be completed. When it is completed it will have cost about $1 million. The greater part of the construction took place two or three years ago.
I understand that the cost for the mechanical end was something like $124,000, but that the extras run up to $245,000. Is that correct? I am speaking of the mechanical and apparatus items only.

I am told that the type of equipment in that building is not only very elaborate but some of it is in the experimental stage, as it will be understood equipment in connection with work of that kind is likely to be. The air conditioning equipment has had to be either reinstalled or considerably changed at a cost of somewhere around $100,000.

I am glad the minister mentioned the air conditioning. I understand that they have some 36 different air conditioning units and that they were installed in such a way that in order to repair one they have to take out 35. I would say that it was elaborate.
Not being an expert on this-
You should be on air conditioning.

Probably I am a better expert on air than on anything else. Nevertheless the kind of work that is being carried on was outlined to us this afternoon by the hon. member for Lambton West. There has not been a great deal of experience with this sort of work in our laboratories or even in our universities. I suppose the professors get new ideas about these things every month. Much of the work being done depends on certain devices, and in the case of air conditioning I can understand how it might have to be changed. However, I am informed that it was not necessary to change 35 in order to get one right. It might have been necessary to change all 35 in order to get any of them right, but you do not have to move one whole group in order to fix another.

My understanding was that they were crowded in a very small space. The minister did not answer my question. I understand that the firm price to begin with was $124,000 and that the extras amounted to some $245,000, but as yet the

apparatus is not functioning the way it should and another $150,000 or more will have to be spent. Is that right or is that wrong?

I am told that what I said is as nearly correct as one can describe it. The amount which was provided last year for this reconditioning work was $100,000. About $60,000 has been expended and what has not been expended will have to be revoted. Then it will take another $50,000 added to what we have already spent to complete the work being done. I am told that in so far as that particular revision of equipment is concerned, when that expenditure is made the equipment will work satisfactorily. As I say, this equipment is associated with experimental work of a type that no one understood completely when they were putting it in. Experience has indicated that some changes have to be made in order to make the equipment work.
That is in order to have air conditioning for the study of entomology?
Largely.
The minister has mentioned equipment that has to be fixed up. As I understand it, it will cost $150,000 before the complete apparatus will function.
I am told that it is not going to cost that much. The officials think the figures I have given represent the cost.

This is the item on which I asked a question in the first place. Would the minister tell us how many buildings are covered in this vote, where they are, how much has been spent for buildings and how much for equipment?
Would it suit the wishes of the hon. member if I were to give the places where these buildings are? There is quite a long description of them here. There are pages of it.
I do not want the minister to read pages of description. Would he give me the total amount expended on buildings, the number of buildings, and the total amount for equipment?
There are seven or eight of them altogether, and the total amount is $1,460,420. They are at Charlottetown, Kentville, Fredericton and so on.
Can the minister divide the amount between buildings and equipment? The item covers both. I should like to have the amount for buildings and the amount for equipment.
The item I am reading just covers buildings.

I presume this item covers the new animal diseases laboratory about which we heard a good deal in the committee established last year to deal with foot-and-mouth disease. I believe it was to be constructed on an island in the St. Lawrence river. Oan the minister tell us if that laboratory has been constructed, what the cost has been and what kind of work has been carried on there?
The building there is not a building that we constructed. It was built by defence. We do carry on some work there occasionally, but the plant there is a defence plant.

I take it, then, that this is a defence plant which the Department of Agriculture has taken over in which to carry on the laboratory work in connection with communicable diseases of animals. I take it that the Department of Agriculture has done some work on it and has put in some equipment. Can the minister tell us what sort of work is being carried on there and what the cost has been to date?

The building and plant there are owned by defence. It was put there in wartime in order to experiment with some diseases which it was thought certain other countries might be spreading within our boundaries. There was an arrangement between the United States and ourselves to conduct that work. That is the reason the buildings were put there. At present we carry on operations in the buildings and plant that are there. Some of our officials are there from time to time to carry on these activities. Some of the activities in connection with the fight against foot-and-mouth disease were carried on at that plant. Our officials went down there and conducted those operations. Any time it is necessary to have officials there, we can send them.

Do I understand the minister correctly that this plant is only in operation as an animal diseases laboratory from time to time when something such as foot-and-mouth disease breaks out, or is it in operation all the time for research on these matters?

It is continuous. It is going on more or less all the time. They may not be as active at one time as at another. That depends upon the diseases we have, but whenever we have any dangerous disease which spreads easily we conduct our work in connection with it there.

Is there any work being carried on there in connection with vesicular stomatitis, which in the beginning was confused with foot-and-mouth disease? I should

How is it administered?

With respect to the other question about the research board, as I remember the history of it the research board was set up in the first place to take over all research work in general. We have representation on the group that considers these matters from time to time. Our deputy would sit in on committees considering these matters. But there are certain problems of research having to do with farming which can only be carried on at our experimental farms right across the country. In so far as it becomes necessary, we quite often do work for the research council, but on other occasions the research council does work for us which we have not the facilities to do. They are asked to do it and they do it.

Forest biology-
13. Operation and maintenance, $1,679,948.
What has been done with respect to the army worm and the budworm?
Experiments are being carried on in connection with the handling of the budworm in Ontario, in Quebec and in New Brunswick.
By your department?

Yes, by our department. When it comes down to the handling of the budworm the provincial governments actually take charge of the work. I understand things like grasshoppers out west a little better, but the principle is the same. We do such work as searching out how the flights are going to take place and so on. We give the provincial governments all the information we can, and the provinces actually put on the battle. That principle applies in connection with the budworm and the army worm. We have not yet found any way of handling the army worm successfully, other than by spraying.
And that is not successful.

It is not as successful as we would like to see it. The reason we do much of the work is that, obviously, you cannot stop these things at provincial boundaries. We must make studies to discover what the movements are and that sort of thing. The information is placed at the disposal of the provinces so they can put on whatever battle is to be waged. The principle applies in respect of all insects.

I believe two years ago the minister said in the house that the army worm would not kill trees. He was absolutely wrong there, because after the army worm has visited oak trees three years in succession the trees are absolutely dead. That is true of birch trees also. In Ontario there are millions and millions of oak and birch trees that have died because of the army worm.

Generally speaking the first statement is correct. An attack of army
[Mr. MacLean (Queens) .1
worm does not usually kill a tree. If you have three attacks in a row I suppose it might, and I am quite certain that if you had five or six attacks in a row they would kill the tree.
One attack won't do it but when they come back-
After one attack the leaves will come back on the trees.
Only part of them.
Enough come back so the tree will live until there is a new supply the next year.

Item agreed to.
15. Plant protection, $779,028.

I notice that most of this vote is for salaries and travelling expenses. I wonder if the minister would tell us what is involved in plant protection. Does it involve such things as research work on rust and smut and things of that sort, or what does it involve?

No. The matters having to do with rust and so on are covered in the experimental farms vote that we will be coming to next. Plant protection here covers checking of plants coming into this country. It is the service you run into at the boundary where they tell you that you cannot bring back in your car some of the things which you might wish to bring in. It is a service that works both ways. It is a protection first for our own country against things coming in, and we have arrangements with our United States friends to the south under which there is protection against plants going the other way. We have some protection against plants being moved to and from European countries.
The most difficult case I have had to deal with since I have been here was when the governor general wanted to send some of our very fine 'mums to his mother in Britain. I do not refer to the present governor general but to the previous one. He took the plants to the airport and they would not accept them on the plane. He asked me to try to make suitable arrangements. I had to explain to him that the difficulty lay not with our regulations but with the British regulations, and we could not get the plants on board.
I take it that this is entirely what might be called an inspection and police operation. There is no research element in it at all?

Yes, it is largely a matter of policing the regulations. For example, seed

potatoes come under this, but rust and similar things come under experimental farms.
Item 15 has nothing to do with spraying plants or with any service in connection with them at all, any treatment of them?
There is a spraying plant at Saint John. It is what they call a fumigation plant, and it is covered in vote No. 15.
If sprays come under this particular item, what work is being carried on to determine the value of different sprays which are on the market for killing weeds?
This vote does not cover the spraying of crops. The spray here refers to that used on plants coming off ships and that sort of thing. The spraying of crops comes under the next vote.

What protection is afforded in connection with the purchase of nursery stock and its movement from one part of the country to another? I am thinking of various tree diseases and the danger of transmitting them from one area to another, especially because there is an outbreak of Dutch elm disease in the United States. I am also thinking of diseases or insects which have almost completely killed the birch trees in the maritimes, necessitating the transfer of certain veneer industries from New Brunswick to Ontario.

There is a co-operative effort between ourselves and the provincial authorities to take care of that matter. As far as we are concerned it comes under this item that we have been speaking about. It would not be possible to say in a few words just what we do. We do different things, depending on the disease that is being looked into and what the nature of the plant is.

I understand that this is the item which deals with the control of various crop diseases, and I would like to ask the minister a question in connection with rust and smut. In the last two or three years I have been quite struck by the amount of smut there is despite the fact that I think farmers universally treat their seed. Despite that treatment-whether it is by dusting or by the old-fashioned formaldehyde method- there seems to be quite a bit of smut on the crops. I wonder what research has been done toward eliminating that condition, which causes a considerable loss as far as yield is concerned and, at the same time, makes grain dangerous for certain uses.

I asked the question under the previous item, but the minister told me it was under experimental farms.
I am sorry. I misunderstood the question.
No matter what item it is under, I wonder whether the minister could say anything with regard to the questions I asked in connection with smut.

As to the question of smut, those of us who are getting seed ready at this time of the year understand the situation fairly well. There are certain methods of handling oats. There are certain methods of handling each of the crops. It is not every farmer who agrees with every other farmer as to what the most effective method is. But there are some well-established methods. Of course, the old one was the use of bluestone which we used on wheat to prevent the development of smut, and it has been extremely effective. There are other forms now-I think what is called mercury dust is one-that are perhaps even more effective than were the old methods. I do not know whether they are more costly or not. I assume that they are.
They are less of a nuisance, anyway. There is less labour involved and they are less of a nuisance.
Yes. There is less labour involved, it can be used more easily and so on. I understand it does not injure the seed at all, and that it is effective.

The minister has not met my point, of course. I said that in spite of the use of these things-formaldehyde, bluestone or these new dusting methods-there is still a considerable amount of smut. In other words the methods do not seem to be completely effective by any means. I was wondering how much research, if any, was being done in evolving something which would get rid of this smut in grain.

Mr. Chairman, I think what the hon. member is referring to is probably

Supply-Agriculture
blue smut in barley, as to which the formaldehyde treatment or the mercury treatment does not produce any results. The only treatment that produces results is the hot-water treatment, which is extremely difficult to carry out on the average farm. I believe some experiments have been carried on to develop a better method than the hot-water treatment. I do not know what stage those experiments have reached or whether there has yet been developed a new treatment for this particular type of smut in barley. I know that experimental work was being carried on in the University of Alberta, because I communicated with them last year with regard to it. However, they had not as yet reached any definite results on it. They were still carrying on experiments. I do not know whether anything new has been developed in the last year with regard to it.
Is this the item under which we can make inquiries about the matter of weed sprays, or is that matter under item 8?

Yes, this is the item. But on the other question that was raised with regard to loose smut, may I say that we have not been able to find any method which is more effective than is the hot-water treatment. The system or the plan that we recommend is to take a comparatively small quantity of the seed, give it the hot-water treatment, and then from that develop seed which is clear of the smut. It is probably too big a job to start to handle all that one might wish to handle from year to year under the hot-water treatment, so one has to build up his seed supply from a small amount that is free of it. That is the method that is recommended.

Can the minister give us some information as to how much experimental work is being carried on in testing these types of sprays which are being brought out every year for the killing of weeds? A great many new ones are coming on the market. Some of them are good and some of them are not so good. Some of them are good for particular weeds, others for general spraying. It is a field in which I am certain that a great deal of experimental work is needed, and I think a great deal of information is needed by farmers who are using those sprays. Sometimes these sprays damage the crops if too heavy a concentration is used.
As to the work that is being carried on by the experimental farms-as I am sure it must be-I think the information which they have obtained should be more widely distributed and made available to farmers. When these new sprays are placed on the market the farmers should know what their

contents are and what their effects will be. Otherwise considerable damage may be caused.

Experiments are being carried on at every one of our experimental farms right across the country with regard to these different sprays. There are 230 different products or sprays being put out. We have publications that we put out to the farmers, indicating the sprays which are successful and the methods that ought to be followed in making the sprays. Most farmers using that method of eradicating weeds follow closely the directions they get. Some, it is true, by not doing so damage the crops.
I understand that about 13 million acres were sprayed last year by some method or other or with some product or other. Most of the spraying has been fairly successful. It does remove a great deal of the weed production. I think the farmers should do what I understand the hon. member for Melfort has been doing. They should write to the different experimental farms or to the agricultural colleges and get advice on the different products they intend to use, and utilize them in the way in which they are directed.

I think this information should be made available in western Canada to municipal councils in such quantities that they can distribute it. I do not think the information which is available in the department is getting out into the proper hands. I would suggest that it be made available to municipal councils, agricultural societies and agricultural committees so that it may get as wide distribution as possible.
As to the other question I asked a little while ago, what stage has been reached with regard to the development of a new rust-resistant wheat, and will it be available for multiplication this year by seed growers in western Canada?

As my hon. friend knows, the plan we have followed for a number of years when we are developing any of the grain products, and particularly wheat, is to take the product that was produced last year and multiply it down in California because we can do it in the winter months and have it ready a year earlier by doing it in that way. We have about 6,000 bushels of the new variety of wheat which was produced last year and which is resistant against the new form of rust-No. 15B-which we have been studying now for two or three years. That wheat has been checked. It is not licensed yet because we have not completely proved the baking value of it, although we think it has a baking value which is just about as

good as any other wheat. In every other way it has proven to be rust-resistant and measures up in every other way except in baking. I should not say "except in baking" because it is just a matter which was not completely proven to the extent of having it certified and put out. But in view of the great damage that might be done if that type of rust were to be here ahead of rust-resistant wheat, we have gone ahead in spite of that fact and we shall have about 6,000 acres seeded to that wheat this year and should have a considerable amount of it for distribution at the end of the season.
Is that being seeded on the experimental farms, or is it being distributed?

It is being seeded largely on land over which we have control. For example, we are seeding some of it on the Bow river project, which is absolutely new land that we are breaking up ourselves for this purpose and which will be utilized as part of the irrigation scheme that is being developed there. It is being put on land over which we have control.
None of it is being distributed to individual seed growers at this stage?

A portion of it will be let out to farmers who have been closely associated with the seed growers' association and whose reputation we are pretty familiar with; but our chief reason for doing it the way we are and trying to keep as much of it as we can on the experimental farms, the irrigation project and places of that kind, is simply that we are not absolutely certain, or were not at the time we made the distribution, with regard to the wheat itself. Therefore we could not guarantee to anyone that we distributed it to that it is right in every particular, so we did not feel that we should put it out under the old plan exactly. The new plan covers any risk that may be taken.

The minister did not answer my question as to whether his department was carrying on any research as far as the smut problem is concerned. If they are not now doing so, I think it would be an extremely valuable project for them to institute. Although we have had this problem a long time and there are different methods of dealing with it, it is by no means solved yet.

If I did not mention it, I intended to. We are carrying on, and have been over a long term of years, experimental work in connection with the fighting of smut, more particularly here, at Winnipeg and at Edmonton. These are the special places at which we are carrying on experimental work.

Of course it is being more or less carried on at all our experimental stations right across the country.

I should like to ask a question which has to do with items 13, 14, 15 and 16. It refers to the dieback disease that has cleaned out birch in the maritime provinces and is now causing great destruction in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. Is the department doing anything in conjunction with the province or on its own to try to control this disease in Ontario?

Yes; it has been the subject of a lot of experimental work. I understand that the disease spoken of, the dieback, or the killing of the tree, starting at the top and coming down, is partly due to disease and partly due to the operations of an insect. They are not absolutely certain either of the nature of the blight or of methods by which to fight it, but work is being carried on in connection with it.
Thousands of acres of birch are being destroyed right in the Haliburton county of Ontario.

I have not taken up much time this afternoon. I want to speak on this item.
I have been sitting here waiting for the opportunity to ask this question. Can the minister tell me what co-operation exists between the manufacturers of the weed sprays and the experimental farms? I think I would be right if I said that the experimental farms will not go so far as to advertise any particular manufacturer's product. We experiment with the implement to find out whether it will do the job it is supposed to do, and we give out information with regard to it. I think we do pretty much the same with these sprays. About all that the experimental farms could say, or are supposed to say, is that they are all products which will give certain results, and they will indicate the results that will be obtained; but as for saying that you should buy this one as against that one, I do not think they would say that.

That is the answer to my question. If there are 200 different sprays we should like to get some guidance from the experimental work that has been carried on, and in that way we would know what one would be the best to use or would give the best results?
There may be quite a number of sprays of that type sold under different names, and they might tell you the type.

I wish to make some observations on this matter, and the minister has now said that he thinks it is the proper place for me to make those observations. I will not be long. My observations have to do with some other items.

I qualified that statement by saying that what I had to say referred to the following four items. However, I do not wish to argue that. I want to introduce my remarks by referring to a statement made recently by the president of the international bank to which Canada has subscribed the amount of $350 million. I would point out that no other member has spoken today about Newfoundland, the part of the country from which I come; and I would draw the minister's attention to the principle involved in the creation of an international bank to help undeveloped countries and remind him that, as I have pointed out frequently before, Newfoundland has suffered for many years from the neglect of its agriculture.
I am wondering to what extent the scientists in his department are giving consideration to the improvement of agriculture in Newfoundland. I notice by the report that they have examined 400,000 acres of land, so far as the survey of soil is concerned. However, that means an area of only about 35 miles by 20 miles and when we realize that the area involved is about 42,000 square miles this portion of 700 square miles is comparatively small.
It will be understood, of course, that I do not expect everything to be done in a moment. Is there any plan or pattern agreed upon between the provincial and federal departments of agriculture regarding the future of that industry in Newfoundland?

Where can one find any statement as to the progress being made in Newfoundland? How many illustration stations will be set up there?
Two have been set up so far, one at Car-bonear and one at Lethbridge. The one at

Carbonear is in the district of Trinity-Conception, and it is fairly centrally located. The one at Lethbridge is in an area where there is some good agricultural land, too. And on that coast they are capable of producing vegetables as cheaply as they can be produced in the maritime provinces. I suggest that those people should have the benefit of an illustration station in order that they may be shown the best methods to treat crops.
Hon. members may not be familiar with this fact, but only recently we had a report from a joint committee which dealt with fisheries development in Newfoundland. It seems to me there should be something of that nature established by the federal government and the provincial government, and applied to the development of agriculture. I do not see how we can make progress if we just carry on as we have before, and do not have any understanding about what should take place in the future. If the minister is in a position to do so, I would ask him to comment on what I have said.
There are four illustration stations in Newfoundland, two of which are on the east coast and two on the west coast.
Would you name them, please?

The one at Carbonear,
established in 1951, is operated by George E. Spore; the one at Lethbridge, established in 1951, operated by James Harris; the one at Doyles, established in 1952, operated by George Cormier, and the one at Heatherton, in the Robinson area, was established in 1952, and the operator is Neil Macdonald.
In relation to the last remarks made by the hon. member, I do not know whether an announcement has yet been made, and in the light of that fact I hesitate to make one, because probably I should not do so. We have already provided Mr. Smallwood with a man who will do the survey and the provincial government, of course, will pay the cost of it. I am glad to know that this is being done. Can the

minister tell us if there is any provision for anything further along the line of the setting up of illustration stations?
We do not intend immediately to set up any more illustration stations. As a matter of fact the investigational work being done will determine to a large extent what we shall do in the future.

I have at times made representations to the minister concerning an experimental station in northeastern Alberta. I understand it will be somewhat difficult to have a station of that kind established on a large scale. I was wondering, however, if the minister would be in a position to give consideration to the establishment of something between an illustration station and an experimental farm in that area.

For some time we have had under consideration the possibility of establishing an illustration station at Vegreville, or in that vicinity. I would not be definite as to the exact location. That is a matter which would have to be looked into further. It was very strongly represented to us, however, that they preferred to have an experimental farm; and that, of course, would be only natural. We did not think we could go so far as to establish an experimental farm in that district, because of the number we already have in Alberta, the nature of the area to be covered, and so on. But we are prepared to establish in the district an illustration station. Of necessity that station would have to be one of our more important illustration stations because of the problems to be handled there. But we would not be in a position to go so far as to establish an experimental farm.

What does the minister mean when he refers to a more important illustration station? What I had in mind was something between an illustration station and an experimental farm, something that would be on a higher level than an illustration station and which could be built up, provided proper support were given. I am sure the support would be given in that area, because the people there are keenly interested in scientific farming methods. I am sure if they were given encouragement, and some help from the federal government, it might develop into an experimental farm. Would the minister care to make any comment?

I do not think I could go so far as to hold out hope that it would be an experimental farm either now or at some other time. However, we do have different types of illustration stations. For example, we go out and rent ten acres of land from a farmer in a district, usually located quite close to some road allowance. We put plots

Supply-Agriculture
there, and invite the public to watch the growth which takes place and watch the experiments from day to day as they drive back and forth. We might have one such station at one point this year and move it somewhere else four or five years hence.
What I had in mind concerning the area to which the hon. member has referred is that because of the nature of that area we have a feeling that something more permanent than what I have described should be established there. If we had, let us say, from 20 to 40 acres, or something of that kind, there might be good reason for having it under some arrangement where it would be more permanent. We might have to buy it, or rent it on a long-term basis, in order to place it in a position where experimental work could be carried on over a longer period of time, and thus give greater stability to the efforts made there.
Is it possible for the minister to give immediate consideration to this matter so the project may be undertaken this summer?

We have already been giving consideration to it and are hopeful of being able to get it started soon.
N&. Herridge: Mr. Chairman, the work of the experimental stations generally is recognized by all. In the interior of British Columbia the work done by the experimental stations has been of great value to the fruit growers and farmers generally. However, the station is located at Summer-land in the Okanagan, where there is mostly dry farming or farming under irrigation. The climatic conditions are different from those that exist in the Arrow lakes and Kootenay lakes sections, where the climate is much more moist.
Even in the Kootenay and Arrow lakes districts we have a great diversity of climate. Often there is a difference of ten degrees within a distance of six miles in winter. The long narrow mountain valleys create quite different climatic conditions in a very short distance. There is considerable industrial expansion in the area and a rapidly increasing population which provides a good market for much of the local production. However, I would say that a large part of the agricultural products consumed in that part of British Columbia have to be imported at the present time.
I am not thinking of the ordinary experimental station, such as they have at Summer-land, but could the minister consider setting up something in a small way so that climatic conditions could be considered, say on the

Upper Arrow lake, where they are quite different from those on the Lower Arrow lake and the Kootenay lake? Then the conditions in the Lardeau valley are different again, because there it is mostly cattle, grain and vegetable production.
Will the minister and his officials give consideration to this suggestion? I am not thinking of anything very expensive. What I have in mind is an arrangement with an established farmer who could be trusted to undertake certain experiments, in many cases related only to a distance of a few miles from his farm.
The hon. member probably knows the station at Creston.
That is quite different.

I imagine that is the type of experimental station the hon. member is thinking of, one that could deal with the particular problems of the area. Of course we are working on that from time to time. I visited Creston last year and was much interested in the work they are doing. It is not an experimental farm in the sense of these large farms, nor is it exactly what we would call an illustration station. It is more in the nature of what I was outlining to the hon. member for Vegreville a few minutes ago, and I can understand that there might be some reason for having similar ones in parts of British Columbia.

I am not even suggesting anything as extensive as the one at Creston, where they are doing an excellent job. A great deal of interest is taken in that illustration station. I am suggesting something even smaller than that because in many cases the area that would be served is relatively small.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a suggestion to the minister and the department. I believe there would be great merit in establishing another illustration station southeast of the Red river in Manitoba. A few years ago the department opened one east of the river and south of Winnipeg. Although that station has been in operation for only two years it is already showing good results. Our handicap before was that the closest experimental farm was the agricultural college in Winnipeg, and then the one at Morden

cn the west side of the river. In the last few years there has been a considerable development in the southeast corner of Manitoba. I hope the minister will see that these illustration stations in Prince Edward Island are given priority, because Prince Edward Island is more of an agricultural province than any other province in Canada as far as population is concerned.

Consideration is given first to the advisability of setting up another illustration station or, second, whether we should move one from where it is to some place else where it would do more good. It may be that we

It has come to my attention that when farmers lose cattle through disease and receive compensation, the compensation they receive is taxable as income in the year of receipt. As the minister will realize, there were several cases in the west last year where men lost their entire herds, received compensation and were not permitted to restock their farms for a certain length of time. That is the case with t.b. and the other disease that I need not mention. How does a man get around the difficulty so far as income tax is concerned? If he receives compensation for all his livestock in this year, for instance, it is all treated as income which he has received, and at the same time he is not allowed to restock his farm in that year.

I do not think that as Minister of Agriculture I can give an opinion on that. It is an income tax matter. I can only say that when we were fighting the foot-and-mouth disease I took the matter up with the income tax people. Individuals took it up with me and I took it up with the department. The only answer I could ever get was that each case must be dealt with on its merits. They said they could not say definitely, when a man received income from the slaughtering of animals, that it was or was not income until they had gone into all the facts in connection with the case. It depended somewhat on what the man was going to do from then on and somewhat on what he had been doing prior to that.
I would not like to say that it either is or is not taxable. I do not think I could say that. The matter would have to be dealt with by the income tax department, and each case would have to be dealt with on its merits. I think that is about all I can say.
It is not quite that easy. It is not the man's fault that he loses his cattle.

I know, but what I am saying is that while I may agree with everything the hon. member is saying I do not make that decision. It is made in the income tax department. It is not really an agricultural matter. It is an income tax matter, and I would not like to say here that any particular individual is not taxable. I think I am taxed too much on some of my earnings even here, but they tax me nevertheless. That is a question that is settled by the income tax people rather than by us.

But I still say that it is the responsibility of the Department of Agriculture to control disease in this country. If it were not for the disease condition the man would not have lost his herd. He would not have received this money, and there would not be anything to tax. I suggest it is up to

the Department of Agriculture in situations of that kind to make arrangements with the income tax branch so the man will not be the loser.
The Minister of Finance is here. He may be able to answer the question. When a man receives compensation for cattle it is definitely generally considered to be income by the income tax branch, and he is not allowed by the Department of Agriculture to restock his farm in that year. Suppose the man loses his herd on account of t.b. at the first of December. He cannot restock his premises until the following year. What happens with the income tax department?

Perhaps the Minister of Finance could answer that much better than I can. However, I would say that if the stock are capital and that is admitted by everyone, then I do not suppose it would fall into a classification that is subject to income tax. But I would not like to say that none of the receipts from cattle slaughtered as the result of having t.b. are taxable. I think every case would have to be dealt with on its merits. My friend smiles, but I sold a bull from my Ontario farm. He was condemned for having t.b. I sent him to market and they took a little gland out of his neck and sold the bull for me. I got just about as much return as I would have got if he had not had t.b. That happens quite often.
I do not know whether it would be classified as something for which I had received income. I presume it would, but there are other circumstances under which it might not be. As Minister of Agriculture I would not like to say that income tax should or should not be paid. I might argue with the Minister of National Revenue as to whether or not income tax should be paid in certain cases and try to settle it that way. I do not think it is my position to make a decision on income tax.
Would the minister answer this question? Was any consideration given to the special cases to which he made reference a few moments ago?

As far as I know none of them paid income tax. I would not like to say definitely that none of them did, but these were cases in connection with the slaughter resulting from foot-and-mouth disease, and I would have to get information from the income tax department about whether any of them paid income tax.
Has the minister received any objections?

No. That is the reason I think they probably did not pay. They wanted,

as my hon. friend wanted, to get a declaration in advance as to whether they would be charged income tax. I could not give it to them because, when I tried to get the information from the income tax people, I was told that every case would be dealt with on its merits. The fact that I have not heard anything about it since would make me believe the people did not pay.
Is the case here not exactly the same as that where a man sells a herd?
No.

The situation is very much the same with the exception, in this case, that the man is not allowed to restock his farm at this time. From the point of view of income tax, if he established his capital investment in the herd then he would not be taxable on the amount.
The point I am trying to bring out is-
