speechtext: I am not in the active practice of law, so I do not give free legal advice.
I wonder if the minister could answer the questions I asked him before in regard to the research carried on in connection with vesicular diseases?
We have not any vesicular exanthema in this country.
No.

And, of course, we will not be bringing any of it here to experiment on it. We would rather follow the experiments on the United States side, keeping in touch with them rather than introducing anything here so we could carry on experiments ourselves. There is some material available here in the event of a possible outbreak. It is available to carry -on work which might have to be carried on, but we are not actually doing research work.

In connection with vesicular exanthema which the minister spoke of, is any knowledge being disseminated to farmers and veterinarians in the country about how to recognize the disease in the event that it does come in from the United States, where it is quite prevalent in a number of states at this time.
This is a disease which had its origin in Africa about 80 years ago, and it has now broken out in California. There are a few cases of it in Idaho and in a section of Utah.
It is also in the New England states.

The United States does not know a great deal about it, and you might say we do not know anything about it because we have had no experience with it. The United States sent samples of the virus to South Africa and a gentleman named Alexander who is a specialist there has gone to California. We have sent men to California to meet him in order that we may obtain whatever information he is able to give with regard to the disease. When we get the information we in turn will make it available to veterinarians here so that they may deal with the disease if it should break out here.

Do I understand that we have no information on this disease in this country at the present time? I mention the matter because I think that hog men recognize it as one of the most serious potential threats to the industry. The disease is already present in a number of states in the United

Supply-Agriculture
States-13, I think-and one or two of those states border on Canada. The disease might very readily be brought into this country, as it is right next door to us at the present time. I think it is a disease against which we should take the most extreme preventive measures in order to keep it from gaining entry into this country.
I am told that the information I gave a moment ago did not apply to the disease mentioned by my hon. friend.
No. It applied to vesicular stomatitis.

To blue-tongue, which is really a sheep disease. It had the African origin. The other disease is more prevalent in the United States than I indicated a moment ago. It has similarities to foot-and-mouth disease and all of our people are pretty well instructed in detecting it in the first place, making a battle against it and seeing that it is confined to wherever the outbreak may come. We have none of it at the present time.

It is very fortunate that we do not have it at the present time, but I was more concerned whether our veterinarian service across the country had been specially alerted to the disease in view of the fact that it is right next door to us; and also as to whether any general information to farmers, hog men and others has gone out in connection with it or particularly whether any information has gone out to them as to what measures they could take to prevent it appearing. I do not know whether or not it is one of those things as to which the way in which you care for your hogs can have any effect on whether it breaks out and develops rapidly. It may be that that is the case.

The veterinary service is alerted to it right across the country. That is the answer to the first suggestion. They are fully alerted to it. I think the very fact that we just had foot-and-mouth disease has alerted everybody on that kind of disease. If one were to see what are really the symptoms of foot-and-mouth disease appear in any animal, I think the first thing he would do is to get veterinary assistance. That is the warning given all across the country. I would hope that no farmer would undertake to fight it himself. Nevertheless the information is available here in publications of one kind or another, and it is sent out to anyone who is interested in it.
That is one of the things I wanted to know. There are publications?

Yes; in order that they
might be informed with regard to the matter. They are the general publications that we put out in connection with animal diseases.

The other question I asked
the minister when I raised the matter previously, and when he asked me to delay it, was as to whether any experimental or research work was going on in connection with this vesicular stomatitis, I think it was, which is similar in its symptoms to foot-and-mouth disease and which is what the foot-and-mouth disease was thought to be when the outbreak first occurred. It would seem to me that it is one of the diseases which, from the evidence we obtained in the committee last year, is much more common than is foot-and-mouth disease. We have had it here in Canada before. That is probably one disease as to which at least some work should be being carried on.

We have had a number of
outbreaks of stomatitis in cattle. The veterinary service across the country knows fairly well how to battle it. We have no cases in Canada at present. There is no report of the disease at all. The methods by which it is fought are fairly well known. As a matter of fact, those methods were applied in the early stages of the battle against foot-and-mouth disease, when it was thought to be stomatitis. The methods used in fighting it are similar to those used in fighting foot-and-mouth disease. The system of quarantine is just as close as is the other, the reason being that the symptoms are similar. However, the cattle recover from the one and they do not recover from the other. That is the difference. If they are kept long enough in quarantine, it can be determined which is which; but they fight it just as strenuously in the early stages as if it might be foot-and-mouth disease.

That is one of the reasons
I raised this matter. The evidence we had in the committee last year was that this was not one of the diseases which required a quarantine to be put on immediately, and that that was the reason the quarantine was not put on for some considerable time last year, namely because it was thought that the disease was vesicular stomatitis. I think it was pointed out in the committee last year that it was a disease which, because of the similarity in symptoms alone, was one in which a quarantine should be imposed immediately. If the regulations have been changed so the quarantine is imposed immediately, I would think that is a good

precaution to have taken. But certainly that was not the situation at the time the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease took place last year.

Unfortunately, or fortunately, it was. Seven different veterinarians said it was stomatitis and that it was not foot-and-mouth disease. Every one of those herds was quarantined. If they all actually were cases of foot-and-mouth disease-and it is presumed they were-and they had not been quarantined, the spread of the disease would have been much greater than it was.
But the quarantine was not put on for some time.

It was put on on the first
day it was reported. Waas's herd was quarantined the first day that it was reported as stomatitis. Our man went right out the first day and quarantined the herd.

But then the quarantine
was lifted.

The quarantine was lifted in a sense some time later, a considerable time later. The quarantine was put on the Burns plant in Regina and that first quarantine was lifted at that time. The quarantine was kept close enough on all of these cases, and surveillance kept close enough that the disease did not spread. But every vesicular case is quarantined the first day it appears, no matter what it is.

I remember that in the committee a year ago there was quite a little bit of discussion on the location of the virus laboratory, and I believe an intimation was given that another site might be obtained for it rather than in Hull. Can the minister say whether another site has been obtained or whether another virus laboratory is being built somewhere else in Canada?
The material all goes to Grosse lie now; that is, all material with regard to dangerous diseases now goes to Grosse lie instead of to Hull.

We lose a great number of cattle each year as a result of shipping fever. Is the department making any special efforts to help control this deadly disease? A great many cattle die of shipping fever. If the disease is caught in time there is not much difficulty; that is, if you can get a veterinarian and can get treatments. But if the cattle are allowed to go two or three days, the situation is serious. It takes only two or three days until they are dead.

Shipping fever is not a disease scheduled under the Animal Contagious
Supply-Agriculture
Diseases Act, for the reason that its prevention depends chiefly on precautions taken in the handling of cattle en route. Complaints received periodically from shippers of feeder cattle in regard to heavy shipping fever losses experienced by them resulted, however, in a departmental decision in September, 1944, to make anti-haemorrhagic septicaemia serum available free of charge, for treatment of cattle passing through or shipped out of central stockyards throughout the country.
Owners, or their agents, of feeder and stocker cattle purchased at public stockyards for further feeding at country points who wish to take advantage of this treatment are required to obtain the services of a qualified veterinarian to inject the serum, and to make application to the local office of the health of animals branch for the serum.
This service, first started at the union stockyards, St. Boniface, Manitoba, as outlined in a notice dated September, 1944, has since been extended to the stockyards at Prince Albert, Saskatoon, Moose Jaw, Regina, Edmonton, Calgary, Lethbridge and Toronto. At the stockyards in Toronto, active co-operation has been given by the provincial department of agriculture by providing veterinary service for injection and by securing reports from the shippers as to the apparent effectiveness of the treatment.
The fact that during the past five seasons complaints in regard to the incidence of shipping fever have been reduced to negligible numbers suggests that this service has been of material help to shippers in reducing losses from this disease. Then information is given here as to the cattle treated at stockyards. The numbers are given and so forth. I do not know whether or not there is any interest in that information.
Is it compulsory that the cattle be treated in transit?
No, it is not.
It should be compulsory. A lot of money is lost in that way. I lost five head two years ago.

Many fruit and vegetable growers in the area in which I live have expressed considerable concern about the validity of the Ontario agricultural products marketing act. Apparently the cause of this concern is the references that were made to the supreme courts of Prince Edward Island and British Columbia, where similar acts were found to be ultra vires.
These acts are important to the growers in our particular area. I am advised by them that they require this type of legislation. They have reason to believe that the Ontario act might also suffer a similar fate were a reference made to the courts on that particular legislation. I understand that there are two schools of thought with regard to amendments. One is that some amendments might be made to the provincial legislation. The other school of thought believes that an amendment might be made to the federal act.
Will the Minister of Agriculture direct the law officers of his department or of the Department of Justice to look into the matter to see whether an amendment might be made in order that the usefulness of this marketing legislation might not be lost to Ontario?

This is a question which comes up as the result of the case in Prince Edward Island. Not being a lawyer, I am not too sure of the legal side of it other than to say the act was declared ultra vires in the courts of Prince Edward Island. The point at issue was taken to the supreme court and it was declared intra vires, and the act was re-established in so far as our legislation was concerned.
My understanding is that what they are discussing in Ontario at the moment is the right to collect fees. There seemed to be some doubt on that question in the decision that was given. The lawyer who conducted the case for the federation in Prince Edward Island was Mr. Milliken of Regina. I was talking to him the other day. I think he is in Toronto now conferring with the Ontario government on the matter.
I doubt very much whether it is something on which we can get a decision from justice that would be very helpful in connection with the matter that is being discussed there.

There is only one place it can be settled, and that is in the courts. As I understand it, if it is questioned in Ontario it would require a case to be taken to the courts in that province, and whether or not the decision was satisfactory, it would have to be carried through to the Supreme Court of Canada to get a final decision in the matter. That is the direction in which they are heading.
The hon. member asks us to go to the Department of Justice. We have already done that. When we had our own legislation passed in this house we got the opinion of justice that it was sound, that it was intra vires. The same opinion has been given with regard to the provincial legislation. There is no other way of settling the question except through the courts. Probably that is the direction in which it will go.

I should like to ask one question in reference to the statement the minister has just made. As far as the dominion act is concerned, the Prince Edward Island judgment decided that the dominion had the right to sell the products of the provinces interprovincially and in the export trade. I believe the finding went farther than that, if my reading of it is correct. The finding said that it was illegal for two provinces to set up a central selling agency to sell interprovincially and in the export trade. Is that correct? My understanding is that the provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island wanted to get the producers of the two provinces together and sell jointly, and the court found that to be illegal under the present act.
If that is so, I think it would be up to the dominion government to amend their act. It should be amended so that two or more provinces could get together and set up a central agency to sell their products, if they have provincial legislation which gives them the power within the provinces, and the dominion legislation gives them the same right in the interprovincial and export trade that they have under the provincial legislation.
These are important points to be cleared up. It is important to know whether the various provincial boards have the right to get together and form central selling agencies to sell in the export and interprovincial trade.

Well, again, I am not an
authority on the matter and I am not going to pretend to advise or say what ought to be done. There is a much better case than the Prince Edward Island case on the question, and that is the old wheat pool case.

When they set up the wheat pools in western Canada they could not set up a wheat pool to take care of the three provinces. They had to have one in each province, and they did have one in each province. Then when they started to set up the selling agency in connection with it they had the pool offices in Winnipeg to handle the grain for all three pools, and the office is still there.
Our wheat board now sits in the wheat pool offices. The name carved in the stone of the building is "pool"; it is not "wheat board". The same staffs that handled the wheat for the old pools now handle the wheat for the wheat board, but that whole set-up was brought about because of the nature of the legislation that is necessary to set up organizations under our federal system. I do not know that any of that has changed very much. I am not too sure that there is anything we can do to overcome the difficulty that exists there.
The other provision that is in the law, as I understand it, is a very short piece of legislation with only a few sections in it. It was drawn up by Mr. Milliken, or he assisted us in drawing it up in the form in which it now is and it was based entirely upon experiences in British Columbia. They had taken their act right through to the privy council, and the privy council had declared it to be intra vires. After that declaration we passed legislation in almost exactly the form that they had taken forward. That is the legislation that was tested in the courts in Prince Edward Island.
As I understand it, in a few words, it gives authority to farmers' marketing organizations set up, let us say in British Columbia, to enforce at least part of the authority which they have to sell, let us say, in the province of Alberta, when they are selling their products there. It makes their operation effective. The one I recall particularly was the saying that no one could market apples in Alberta, except under certain conditions. Even the Alberta farmers' co-operatives questioned that. They thought an individual in British Columbia should have the right and, under our system in Canada, did have the right to ship apples from British Columbia to Alberta, to anyone. And, having shipped them through, they said the Alberta co-operative could sell them. That was the matter they desired to overcome so they could enforce their legislation not only in British Columbia but in Alberta as well. And I understand that the legislation does make that kind of thing possible.
The other matter, as to whether you can set up a board and give it all the authority 68108-292
Supply-Agriculture
in two provinces that it would have in one, in order to bring commodities together for sale-well, I would not like to offer an opinion as to whether it can or cannot be done.

The minister referred to the central selling agencies and the pools as an example of what I have suggested. But the central selling agency was set up before we had our present marketing act. So far as I know it was never challenged in the courts. The central selling agency continued to sell, and no case was taken to the courts challenging their right to do so.
If my reading of the findings in the Prince Edward Island case is right, a definite ruling was made there that the provinces did not have the right to set up a central selling agency. Personally I think that is something which, if it is a fact, could be remedied. I would ask the minister to inquire into the matter; because I certainly think our marketing act should be amended so the provinces would have that right. And I suggest it would be up to the dominion government to provide such a right; I do not think the provinces can do it. It must be done by federal legislation.
For instance, the honey producers in Saskatchewan have a board. The Manitoba people are voting on one. I am not sure as to the situation in Alberta, but no doubt they will have one at some time. It seems to me that a central selling agency for the three provinces for the purpose of selling honey would be of great advantage to the producers of honey in those provinces, just the same as the central selling agency of the wheat pools has been beneficial to the wheat producers in western Canada. I think something should be done in this connection.
Then there is one other matter about which I should like to make some brief comment. I hold in my hand the brief the Canadian Federation of Agriculture presented to the government, in which they say:
Our convention endorsed the policy of sale of farm products by grade and we urge the federal government to see that where products are sold by producers on grade, the grade identification is carried through to the consumer.
That is a very important point, and at the present time I do not know of any machinery in the Department of Agriculture which actually stipulates that grades received by producers for different products graded under dominion and provincial regulations are carried through to the consumer. In fact, in connection with a good many products, the grades under which they are sold to the consumer are different altogether from the

Supply-Agriculture
grades indicated when the producer markets his product.
For instance, when the (producer kills beef, there are a number of grades which would apply: choice, good, medium, cows, canners and cutters, perhaps ten or twelve different grades. But when that beef reaches the consumer it appears under only two labels, red label and blue label. The packer buys the beef as, perhaps, medium, good or choice. And if he is able to chisel a bit on the grade given the farmer, medium beef may reach the consumer as red label.
The same reasoning applies to eggs and various other products. There are certain standards under which the producers sell. But we have no knowledge as to whether the people who in any given period of time may buy 100,000 cases of grade A eggs, may not sell to the consumers in that same period of time 125,000 cases of grade A eggs. There is no protection either to the producer or to the consumer, unless someone takes the responsibility of seeing that the grades credited to the producer are carried through to the consumer.
It seems to me this is a function which should be carried out by the marketing branch. I would ask the minister to give us an indication as to what is being done in that connection.

In so far as beef is concerned, it is true that there are only two grades of beef which are enforced, namely red and blue brand. As has been said, if a man sells an animal alive to someone on the market and that animal is slaughtered, it is not graded until it is slaughtered. But there is nothing to prevent anyone who wishes to have the matter of grading enforced, insisting upon having the same thing being done with beef as is done with hogs, and that is to have it sold on the rail, dressed. He could do that; and if he did he would see to it that the grades were carried right through from the producer to the consumer. But only those two grades are affected in that way by the present grading regulations.
Going on to other products, we see for example that butter is stamped right on the package. Cheese is graded, and the grade is indicated right on it in so many places that it would be difficult for anyone to tamper with that grading. Many products are graded in that way.
Then, as the hon. member has said, the grading of eggs in Saskatchewan is a controversial matter. It is a situation peculiar to Saskatchewan as compared with the other provinces because, so to speak, we are sitting on the roof of matters having to do with

trade in commodities of that kind. We are farthest away from the market, and we have the smallest market in relation to the production throughout Canada.
Coming to the handling of eggs, the fact is that the great proportion of eggs in Saskatchewan are just taken in as nest run, and sold in that way. It stands to reason that those eggs will not bring as much as graded eggs would bring. But eggs can be graded, and there are many grading stations even in Saskatchewan. When eggs are taken to the grading stations and graded, they can be sold under the marketing plan we have, and under the supports now obtaining, at exactly the same level as graded eggs are sold elsewhere. But we do run into difficulties because we have no storage facilities and there are other things that we have not as well.
I have said many times in Saskatchewan, and I want to repeat it here, that that part of it is provincial. If the province does nothing about it-I am not now speaking about any particular government or any particular form of government; it does not matter what form it is-there is nothing we can do about it. If we set up a system under which it is possible to get 30 cents a dozen for eggs, there is no way the producer can get that 30 cents a dozen unless somebody who has the authority to enforce it does so. The question has been raised here today once or twice about the price of beef in the butcher shop as compared with the price of the animal. If an animal is taken into a butcher shop in Ontario, sold to the butcher and then he sells the beef to the consumer, this government has nothing to do with that, except in wartime.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We were considering item No. 30.

I shall detain the house only for a minute or two. I wish to express my support of the remarks made by the hon. member for Melfort just prior to the six o'clock recess in connection with the necessity for amendment of federal marketing legislation and the inspection of farm products at the consumer level. I think there is no question about it that since the decision of the supreme court of Prince Edward Island the present federal marketing legislation has proved to be inadequate to serve the purpose that was intended. Personally I think that

amendments are necessary. I am not only expressing my own opinion but also that of many farmers who are interested in the development of marketing board legislation. Amendments are necessary to strengthen the law and provide legislation that will permit co-operation between the various provincial marketing boards to ensure proper control and regulation of the marketing and distribution of agricultural commodities.
I also support the remarks of the hon. member with respect to the necessity for more inspection of farm products at the consumer level. I know that in a good many cases in British Columbia, for instance, eggs are inspected in the stores by inspectors of the minister's department. But I do think that such farm commodities as bacon and beef are often sold without consumers knowing the grade they are buying. That also applies to vegetables to quite an extent. I wish to bring to the minister's attention particularly the fact that fruit is very frequently sold without the consumer having any idea what grade of fruit he is buying. Right in Ottawa I have seen British Columbia apples transferred to other boxes and sold without any grade marking, with the result that the consumer does not actually know the grade of apples or other fruit that he or she is buying.
I think that is a serious matter and I believe some consideration should be given to it, because the growers of British Columbia -and Ontario and Nova Scotia growers have learned to do the same thing from our example and experience-pack fruit according to grade and pack it as well as it is done anywhere in the world. When growers' organizations go to the trouble of grading and packing fruit according to the law and above the standards required by the Department of Agriculture, I think it is a shame that the consumer does not obtain the advantage of that grading and packaging.
When the minister was speaking about inspection of eggs I thought I heard him say that in Saskatchewan a farmer can take ungraded eggs to a store and sell them. I should like him to tell me if I heard him correctly.
That is correct.
Thank you.

I understand there is no legislation to enforce grades. If I may make myself plain, taking hogs, which are a pretty good example, if a hog is a pound too heavy there is nothing in the law compelling the packer to put that hog outside the bacon type. In other words, he just passes it through. He is at liberty to put bacon hogs into any grade 68108-2921
Supply-Agriculture
he likes when he gets them, and also other products, but the bacon hog is a typical example.

We have the Livestock and Livestock Products Act and the provincial governments have the same kind of law. The grade qualifications are established under that law, and they are based upon weight. When a hog reaches a certain weight it is outside A grade. The next classification is B, and hogs of certain weight remain within B classification. Otherwise the hog becomes a heavy or light depending upon the weight at which the hog weighs in. Therefore the grade is established by the act or by regulation under the act, and that is the grade by which the packer abides, and everyone else who is buying and selling.
But you never see any grade B bacon.

There is grade B bacon. I think I have mentioned this before, but I was associated for a long time with Mr. Dunning who, as you know, was closely associated with all the farm organizations a few years ago. I happened to be in Great Britain with him in 1936. As you also know, he was born in England, and one Sunday he went to visit his relatives. When he came back on Monday he said, "You know, I was quite surprised to find that everybody on the farm here talks about exactly the same things as they do back in Canada." I said "What do you mean by that?" He said "They spent the week end telling me that all the hogs m Britain go in as low grades, B's or C's but they all come out of the plant as A's! which is exactly the same thing we hear back in Canada." I think that is probably a usual statement to be made, but there is a relationship between the hogs that go into the bacon of different types and the bacon that comes out of the shop. I think most of us take care of that. If we do not get the right grade from one packing plant we probably buy from another.
I can understand that, but there is no legislation in the dominion to enforce these grades so that they must be carried through.
I think the hon. member is quite right that there is no grade of bacon established by law which you can absolutely compel someone to deliver to you.

I ask this question because I had a lot of complaints around Christmas time about the turkey business. The farmers go and sell their turkeys and they get so many B's and C's and very few A's. Then when they go into a big store and are able to identify the birds they sold they find that

Supply-Agriculture
most of them are A's. If a farmer has only produced a B bird then he is not entitled to any more, but the consumer should then get the benefit instead of the packer marking it an A bird.

Again we come back to the point the hon. member started out to discuss, namely who has the authority? The fact is that a case was taken to court and it was determined that the legislation was ultra vires of the dominion to enact. All that means is that the province has the authority to enact it. Everything that can be enacted by anyone can be enacted by either the dominion or the provinces, and if a court decides that we do not have the right to do it then the province has the right. That is all that means.
With respect to the purchase of a dozen eggs in the province of Ontario, if the eggs are bought from an Ontario farmer and sold to an Ontario consumer the federal government has nothing to do with that transaction. We cannot say how the eggs must be graded; we cannot say what the price should be; and we cannot insist that there be a certain margin as between the purchase price and the sale price. We have no authority to do that, but the province has. Sometimes the province does it and sometimes it does not. With respect to some products they do it and with regard to others they do not.
One of the unfortunate things about the matter is that including the period of the war, for ten years of the lifetime of most of the people who are buying in stores-and ten recent years in that period-we did have control. We said what the price of eggs would be for a certain grade. We established the grades and we established that practice in business; and it is hard for us to convince people that what we did for ten years we cannot still do. The fact is, however, that if we attempted to do it today we would be taken into court and eventually our action would be proven ultra vires, so we would not be any further ahead than when we started.
The law with regard to these matters must be passed by the provinces. When you come to the matter of inspectors, we have inspectors and the provinces have inspectors. We have a law and the province has a law with regard to grading, and with regard to the purchases that are made in accordance with the grading. One way we overcome the difficulty is that we appoint all the provincial inspectors as our inspectors and the provinces appoint all our inspectors as their inspectors. When a man makes an inspection he may be an employee of the provincial government; but if the transaction is between two people, one living in one province and one living in

another, while he is making that inspection that inspector is working for the federal government. If it is the other way around, and if the transaction is one between two persons in the same province, then the same man may make the inspection and he is then acting for the provincial government. Even if he were our inspector he would be acting for the provincial government. We have had regulations like that for a long time with regard to butter, cheese and all of these products, and it has been declared in court that we can operate on that basis without getting into legal difficulties. That is why we operate in that manner.
I sometimes run into difficulties and some of our own members write to me and ask why so and so prosecuted a case in such and such a town. Someone may be thinking in terms of political patronage, and would want to know why a Tory lawyer handled the case. I look into the matter and find that the case was brought by one of our inspectors acting for the government of the province of Ontario, and they employed a Tory lawyer to prosecute the case in court. All these complications run through the different activities connected with these matters.
In the province of Saskatchewan I have not found a C.C.F.'er-and I am now talking to some of them-who will admit that they have the authority there to pass legislation having to do with the price of eggs. Well, there is no one else who has that authority. If the government of the province of Saskatchewan will not pass the legislation and will not set up a board to handle the matter, there is nothing anyone else can do about it.
It was quite correctly stated here this afternoon that in the province of Ontario they are having some discussion about whether their boards are intra vires. They have 17 boards. They took a vote with regard to eggs but it did not go through, although they have boards with regard to a lot of other things. One of the boards handles the marketing of hogs in Ontario, another board handles the marketing of cheese, and so on. Under the provincial law they have set up the 17 boards, and the board concerned establishes the price of cheese, for instance.
My hon. friend for Huron North I think said something about the price of cheese recently. Well, recently the price in Ontario has been higher than it has been for some time. I cannot take credit for it; I had nothing to do with it. The provincial government set the price of cheese and said what it was going to be. They set that price and gave authority to the producers' board in Ontario to take all of the cheese. Last

year they did take delivery of the cheese and I believe they sold it for 30 cents a pound. That price was established by the provincial government and it was enforced by the provincial government. If we had attempted to do that we would have been taken into court and our action would have been declared ultra vires.
I am again saying there is a way of controlling these matters. The provincial government can do it. It was first started in British Columbia and they have it pretty well established there now. Ontario has been doing it more recently and the practice is pretty well established there. However, in the province of Saskatchewan, where that type of activity in connection with marketing really started a long time ago, there is a lot less of it being carried out today than in any other province of Canada.
As usual, the minister got up to answer a question about grades and he switched the whole thing over and talked on prices for about ten minutes.
I have not been talking about prices; I have been talking about who has control over grading.

I asked about grades, but this has been a different proposition altogether. As far as eggs in the province of Saskatchewan are concerned, while those consumed in the province might be controlled, unfortunately 70 to 80 per cent are marketed outside the province.
It is the other way around.
I am speaking of the ones that go to market. I am not speaking of those eaten there.
There are more eaten locally than go to market.

The Canadian Federation of Agriculture is asking for something reasonable. They are asking that the producers and consumers both be protected and, when a grade is given to the producer on a particular product, they ask that it be carried through to the consumer. I know that it would take co-operation between the province and the dominion. There are a lot of agricultural products that go into interprovincial trade; and when any agricultural product goes into interprovincial trade the grading of that product becomes the responsibility of the federal government. Under dominion legislation the responsibility in connection with the marketing of the product in that grade rests with the dominion.
I think there has been a lot of co-operation, as the minister has stated, between the provinces and the dominion in the matter of grading; and it is just common sense to carry that
Supply-Agriculture
co-operation a little further, and for the dominion and the provinces to get together and pass the necessary legislation so these grades can be carried through to the consumers. The producers in this country are anxious to see that the consumers are protected.
The grade is carried through to the consumer on eggs.
I am not talking about eggs.
You are talking mainly about eggs.
There are a lot of products besides eggs. The minister says the grades are carried through on eggs, but they are not checked on eggs.
They are.
What check have you in the provinces? Let the minister sit down until I finish asking the question.
You have done a lot of talking about eggs-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
You have asked me a question, so let me answer it. The grade is marked right on the crates in which you buy the eggs.
Just a moment. The people who purchase eggs purchase them under dominion grades.
No, not necessarily.

Well, let us say they are purchased under grades set up co-operatively between the provinces and the dominion. As I said earlier this afternoon, there is nothing I know of in the law, nor are there any checks made, to ensure that a company which purchases perhaps 100,000 crates of grade A eggs does not sell 110,000 crates of grade A eggs to the consumers; in other words that they do not place grade B eggs in with grade A eggs. They may undergrade to the producer and overgrade to the consumer. There is no check on it.
There is a check at the grading stations. They go through the grading stations.

There is no check made to see that the consumer gets what the producer has been paid for, either in respect of bacon or in respect of any of the other agricultural products. No check is made. I might refer, for instance, to butter. No check is made to see that only grade 1 cream is used in the production of grade 1 butter. That is what the Canadian Federation of Agriculture are asking for. I am certain that this legislation can be passed and can be made effective if

Supply-Agriculture
there is co-operation between the province and the dominion in the putting into force of the regulations. There has been co-operation in the setting of the grades. There is co-operation in the appointing of the inspectors. If that co-operation is carried one step further I think both the producer and the consumer can be protected; but I do not think they are being protected at the present time. If they were, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture would not be passing a resolution like this and presenting it to the government.

The Canadian Federation of Agriculture passed a general resolution. Of course they discussed it with the government when they came in. As long as you stay with that general resolution I will agree with you 100 per cent that there is a reason for having the resolution. But when you start to try to apply it to eggs-
I did not apply it only to eggs.
The hon. member told me to sit down. I will tell him to sit down for a while. When you start to apply it to eggs and then you turn right over-
The minister should address the chair.

I addressed the chair when I rose, and I am still addressing the chair. When you start to talk about eggs and then mix with them bacon as though you were eating bacon and eggs instead of dealing with the product on the market, you are doing something that should not be done. You just cannot deal with them both in the same way. Anyone will admit that you can grade eggs, put them into a box, say that they are grade A, and can follow them right through to the consumer. But if you start to do that with slices of bacon, it is not quite so simple. The date of the production of the eggs and everything can be stamped on them, if the regulation calls for it, and quite often it does. The people who want to conform most closely to it, and prove that they are doing so, even stamp the date of the egg on the egg itself and put them into the box. Of course you can follow them through. You would find ways of following them through, and there are ways found for following them through.
When anyone says the province itself does this or the federal authority does that, may I say there is co-operation between the province and the federal authority in the matter of grading. But that co-operation does not follow out of the one province into another, except for the fact that all eggs are graded by inspectors who are inspectors of both governments, provincial and federal, so you cannot miss on it. But in so far as those eggs

that are bought in the province and sold in the province are concerned, if the grade does not follow right through that is entirely the responsibility of the provincial authorities. They have to police it and see that it is carried right through. If it is a matter of trade as between one province and another, then we can join in the policing of it.
But there are some difficulties even in that, once the product is sold to somebody who lives in another province. But when it is sold in Ontario and becomes the property of someone who lives in Ontario, when he sells it to somebody else it is one provincial citizen selling to another. He is selling a product which became his property; and under the matter of civil rights we are in difficulties again if we get mixed up in enforcing it. The people who enforce these things are the provincial people, not the federal people. Unless the people in a province will agree to it and go ahead and do it, it just cannot be enforced.
That is all I have to say about it, and I continue to say it because I know I would just run into difficulty if I tried to say anything else.

Mr. Chairman, the main
trouble that I notice with regard to eggs is that whilst they are graded when they are purchased from the farmer-the farmer, in order to get grade A for his eggs has to sell fresh eggs-when the consumer buys them, he has no guarantee at all. I have never bought a dated egg yet. As a matter of fact, as to any eggs I have bought, I am sure they have not seen their mother for many, many weeks. It seems to me that when eggs are sold the date should be stamped on them so the person buying them knows whether they are one week old, two weeks old, or maybe a month or two old.
As a matter of fact the eggs are graded into a storehouse, into a cold storage. We grade them out. Every egg that goes into cold storage, that is graded in, we grade out.
There is no date on them.
We grade them out, and we grade them as to whether they are grade A or some other grade.
They may stay in the shop for a week or two.

We have graded them out when they have been in six months, not a week or two; and if they are stored properly and under the right conditions, they come out in the same form as that in which they went in. That was not so simple to do some

time ago as it is in these times. My friends from British Columbia have been claiming for a long time that they have discovered a system of dipping eggs in oil which keeps them fresh. I have been told over in Britain by a member of the government that when they had a shipload of these British Columbia eggs come over to Britain, a fresh egg laid in the morning in Britain was put on his plate along with an egg that came from British Columbia; and even this minister of the government-and they are usually as well informed as anybody and their tastes are about as good as anybody's-could not tell which egg was laid in Britain that morning and which egg was laid in British Columbia some weeks earlier.
He had lost his sense of taste.

That has all been tested. What I am saying to my hon. friend is that eggs can be put into storage, can remain there for weeks and months, and can be taken out and graded as they were graded when they went in, and you would have difficulty in determining what date they were laid.
Mr. Chairman, may I say a word?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Kootenay West.

Mr. Chairman, I was greatly interested in the minister's explanation of the constitutional position of an egg inspector in the performance of his duties. It is rather perplexing, but as a result of his explanation I want to ask him a question. If the dominion egg inspector is inspecting in British Columbia eggs that have been imported from Alberta-
They would be good eggs.
They are all good eggs.

-and if there is a complaint against the work of that inspector, then I presume the complaint should be made to the dominion government. But if he is inspecting eggs that were produced by a local poultryman and sold in a local store, then I understand he is an employee of the provincial government. Am I then to understand that the complaint should be addressed to the provincial agriculture department?
No. I think you will find that what your people claim is this, or more particularly your fruit people when you are talking about fruit-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You are now talking about eggs.

It is the same thing, I guess.
Supply-Agriculture
Hen fruit.

When you are talking about fruit that come in from Washington, when the fruit comes in and is the property of somebody living in British Columbia, you claim that you should have the right to pass on it. That is a transaction between two individuals and therefore is within the authority of the province. The same thing would be true when the eggs come from Alberta. This is my kind of law. It may not stand up in a court, but there are a great many lawyers who do not make their laws stand up in court either. I will give it to you for what it is worth. When the eggs come in from Alberta, if they still belong to somebody who is living in Alberta and he is trying to sell them in British Columbia, then in theory it is our inspector who must inspect those eggs and make a report upon them. But if the eggs have been sold to somebody in British Columbia, and he starts to resell them to somebody else, that probably would have to be taken care of by the provincial inspector. He might be the same fellow in both cases, and he might be acting for the province when he is doing one job and acting for the dominion when he is doing the other.
I have had complaints about inspectors acting in these circumstances.
I am quite sure you will have a complaint in any case; and I am not sure, without knowing all the facts, where you would make it.

I want to ask a different question about eggs. The whole problem has been solved in Kootenay. They put them in oil and they go to England two weeks or two months later, but in the Fraser valley the eggs are laid with a date on them so you know what you are getting. We have a special kind of hen out there.
Oh, oh.

We have eggs for over there, too-duck eggs. Has consideration ever been given to selling eggs by weight instead of grade A, B, C and so on? I remember one occasion, Mr. Chairman, when we discussed something other than wheat in the committee on agriculture. I believe it was the first time in 13 years that we discussed anything else but wheat in that committee. At that time we were outvoted because five members either were doctors or they sold feed grain to the farmers. They voted against us. These are the facts. When you get seven or eight lawyers and feed grain men on the agriculture committee you may as well have no committee at all.

Supply-Agriculture
Bananas and oranges are sold by weight, and the housewife knows what she is getting. She knows that she is going to get a certain quantity of bananas or oranges for a certain number of cents. I believe in Saskatchewan at the present time they have the same system of inspection that we have. I will change that, and say that in the last six months perhaps our system of inspection has been worse than what they have in Saskatchewan. Normally when we ship eggs to the feed companies in British Columbia that handle most of'the eggs, they are sent in four grades from the farm to the big feed companies or the packing companies that handle the farmers' eggs. In our province the farmer gets a very small percentage of the eggs credited to him as grade A. The majority are credited as grade B or cracks. I have forgotten what the other names are.
Pullets.
I am getting advice from a city farmer behind me. There are other grades that have colours or spots in them.
You are talking about roosters' eggs.

No, and I am not talking about the turr's eggs that you have in Newfoundland, either; I am talking about hen's eggs. If eggs were sold by weight I believe the big feed and packing companies would not be able to gyp farmers as they are doing now, and they are doing it in British Columbia and even in Ontario the good, or the province that used to be good before it adopted Ottawa or some of the civic officials, at least.
I am afraid I am covering a lot of ground in what I am saying. I will even take in Nova Scotia. They pulled out their apple trees because they could not grow apples. They had to buy them from British Columbia. Has the minister's department given consideration to selling eggs by weight? It seems to me that everything we do not want to do, we say it should be done by the provinces. Does this have to be done by the provinces, or has the federal authority power to compel the provinces to do it?

It is done now. There are four grades of eggs. There is the extra large, the large, the medium and the small. There are minimum weights in all these grades. Grade A extra large has to be 27 ounces. Grade A large is 24 to 27 ounces; grade A medium 21 to 24 ounces and grade A small 18 to 21 ounces. In other words, when you buy grade A extra large eggs you know the weight is at least 27 ounces, and the others are as I have read them. The margin
(Mr. Cruickshank.]
between the top and the bottom is not very great. You do not get an absolute guarantee that every egg weighs so and so, but you have a guarantee that it is within a very small range. That has been dona for some time.
For the benefit of my hon. friend may I say that if we were going to have British Columbia eggs sold in British Columbia it would still be the province that would do the enforcing; but if it happened that Alberta eggs were being sold to somebody in British Columbia by somebody in Alberta, well, it would be the same man who would inspect but he would be working for us when he did it.

I thank the minister for his information. Of course he did not understand what I was getting at, so perhaps I shall have to move into the Department of Agriculture. He has not answered my question at all. I am getting so much advice from Springfield and elsewhere that do not produce eggs that I say to them if they want to make a speech they will have an opportunity to do so.
I will make mine after you are through and they will understand it.
If they understand you they will understand anything.
Who is the parliamentary assistant now?

What I am getting at, Mr. Chairman, is this. I am afraid the minister did not get my point. These eggs are sold as grade A, so many ounces and grade B, so many ounces, but I can take the minister downtown tomorrow in the fair city of Ottawa and he will be sold eggs by the dozen grade A, or grade B.
But they must weigh so much.

Exactly. But bananas are not sold as grade A; they are sold by the pound. If eggs were sold by weight the housewife would get full value, and what is more important the farmer would get full value. But when they go down to the packing plant-and I think this is true in Saskatchewan, too-the farmer does not get full value because the packer grades so many as grade A, so many ounces to the dozen, and others are graded grade B, so many ounces to the dozen. But the average packing plant will give the farmer credit for a larger number of grade B's than grade A's. That is an altogether different matter from selling them by weight.

The answer to the other part of the question is this. Where the price is

set on fruit it is done provincially; it is not federal.
The same thing is true of eggs.

It could be on eggs or anything else, but I am just saying to you now that it must be provincial. When the transaction is between the storekeeper and the customer coming into the store and buying something, if the law can be enforced at all it must be a provincial law. It does not matter whether it is fruit or eggs you are talking about. When you go into a store in the province where the law exists to that effect, then you buy it by the pound; and you can buy eggs by the pound in the stores here, too.
Where?
Any place, if you insist.
No, you cannot.

I am a farmer and I am accustomed to eating fresh eggs. We get good eggs in this House of Commons. First of all may I say that all the food we get in this building is the very best. Not so long ago I was having breakfast with a certain gentleman and he had two fried eggs. He said to me, "You are a farmer. Do you not eat eggs?" I said: "Yes, I do when I am at home." He said: "Why don't you eat them here?" I said: "Well, you are not eating fresh eggs." He said: "How do you know I am not?" I said: "I know by the look of them." He said: "Why are they not fresh eggs?" I said: "When you drop a fresh egg into a hot pan it will whiten right over the yolk." You cannot whiten the yolk of a stale egg. There is nothing wrong with the egg, any more than that it is not fresh. And when one is accustomed to eating fresh eggs, one that is four or five months old does not taste the same. That is all I wish to say about that subject.
Then I wish to register a complaint in connection with the committee on agriculture. It is one of the most important groups in Canada. I have been in the House of Commons for 13 years, and I know that in some sessions we do not have even one meeting of that committee. If I were Minister of Agriculture I would want to have the committee sit.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I am sorry to have to interrupt the hon. member, but I think the scope of the discussion is wide enough. I do not think we ought to go into a matter which is completely extraneous to the item under study. The hon. member could have made his suggestion during the discussion 68108-293
Supply-Agriculture
on the first item. I realize that his remarks may be prompted by the suggestion to the same effect by the hon. member for Fraser Valley. However, I do not think we should proceed with a discussion at this time as to whether or not the committee on agriculture should sit more often.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I shall have to bow to your ruling, but I have always understood that the committee on agriculture is to assist the Minister of Agriculture. Why does it not hold more meetings? Today was the first time this session that a meeting of that committee was held.

To back Mr. Chairman's ruling, let me say that I am not too sure that the statement just made is correct. I am not on the committee on agriculture, and there is no particular reason why I should be. That committee is set up by the house, and the matter now before it, and that has caused it to sit at this time, did not even arise in my department.
That is the point I would like to make.

It is a matter of trade and commerce. And while I would be quite prepared to discuss the question as to whether there have or have not been meetings of the committee on agriculture, I think it would be entirely out of order to do so here. It has nothing to do with my estimates at all.
Why is not legislation sent to the committee on agriculture?

I wish to set the hon. member for Fraser Valley right. He has been sitting in the House of Commons for 15 years as a representative of the farmers, and it is quite evident to me that he does not know what goes on in connection with the grading of eggs. I want to put him straight, and also I would do the same for the hon. member for Melfort. I have a sister in Saskatchewan who has quite a number of hens. This egg grading is done right at home. There is a scale on which these eggs are weighed- grade A large, large, medium and small. Furthermore, after the eggs are weighed they are all candled, stamped with a date placed upon them. When one goes to a store in Saskatoon to buy eggs, he knows exactly the date they were laid and the date they were packed. And to make it even clearer to my hon. friend from Fraser Valley-
And to yourself.

-if he goes to the store and buys a dozen grade A large eggs, and pays 68 cents for them, he will get so many ounces

Supply-A griculture
to the dozen. For large eggs he will pay about 65 cents and receive so many ounces to the dozen. Medium eggs he will buy for perhaps 61 cents, and again they will weigh so many ounces to the dozen. Small eggs are sold in the same way, possibly for 55 cents. So it is clear that he buys his eggs by weight when he is buying according to grade. Now do you understand that?
I wish to express my appreciation to my hon. friend and colleague who sits behind me-
Your parliamentary assistant.
-for putting me correct. Only he does not know what he is talking about; that is the only trouble.

I have listened with much interest to this discussion about eggs. Coming from a constituency which probably produces more eggs than any other in Canada, I thought I was fairly familiar with the subject. However, after listening to hon. members I have come to the conclusion that I know absolutely nothing about the grading of eggs.
As I understand it, a producer can grade his eggs and sell them locally. I know that down in my part of the country there are many grading stations, and these grading stations are licensed. Who grants the licences for them? In those stations there are certain people who grade the eggs. Then the eggs are shipped to the cities and are placed in storage. I would ask the minister if they are graded when they go into storage and, if so, who grades them.
Then if I understand the minister correctly he said, "When they are taken out of storage, we grade them." I take it from what he says that when they are taken out of storage they are graded by an inspector of the federal Department of Agriculture. If I am wrong in that I would ask the minister to correct me. I should like to know very definitely who grades them when they go into storage and who grades them when they come out.

In Ontario the egg stations are authorized or registered by us to grade eggs. The other activities in relation to eggs are the same as in other provinces. In the western provinces the provincial governments issue the licences to the stations. Their system is somewhat different from that in Ontario. But in both cases the reason for our being in it at all is that some eggs are graded from one province to another, and some go to other countries. All eggs are graded under that same system, whether they are sold in the province or outside of it.
Who grades them when they go into storage and when they come out?

The eggs are graded into storage by the station. We supervise the grading in of the eggs. We also supervise the grading out of the eggs. The eggs are graded by the operator of the station which takes them.
I understand the graders in the local stations receive some training before they are allowed to grade eggs. Is that supervised by the federal or provincial government?

We supervise grading; but if there were any legal questions brought up in connection with it we could not enforce the sale according to our grades, within a province. But we do supervise grading of eggs both in and out.
And your inspectors inspect them?
Yes.

I think it is clear from the contributions made by most members to this discussion that the grading of eggs in the country is not satisfactory, so far as the producer is concerned. Whether the grading is good or not, it appears that the result to the producer is an unsatisfactory price. I think one of the greatest difficulties in connection with eggs is the fact that, as in connection with so many other products, we are confined to the Canadian market; and that market is not always sufficient to take care of all the eggs produced in Canada, so as to return a reasonable price.
There may be another item under which the question I want to ask might be more appropriate and, if so, I do not mind waiting for an answer. I should like to have the most recent figures with regard to the quantities of agricultural products the government now holds. Then there is a further question I should like to ask about eggs. I would like to know what quantities of eggs have been purchased by the agricultural prices support board or the agricultural products board; how many eggs are on hand now, and what disposition was made of the eggs.
