How many eggs has the department purchased at any time during the last twelve months?
We purchased 39,000 cases in 1953 and sold them.
What was the egg production in 1952?
We lost about $53,000 in that particular instance.
Have you the total egg production in Canada for 1952?
The total number of eggs marketed through egg stations was about five million cases.
And you purchased 39,000 cases?
Yes.
In what provinces were those eggs purchased?
I have not the exact division, but most of them came from Saskatchewan, with some from Manitoba.

I understand that the grading and inspecting of potatoes is done by the federal government and I should like to know if that inspection and grading would be binding when shipments were made to another province. That is, if a shipper had his potatoes graded, inspected and tagged and sold them in Ontario, would the buyer there have to accept that grading or could he call in another inspector and have them regraded?
Supply-Agriculture

Yes. When potatoes are shipped from one province into another there is a check made by one of our inspectors on the grade in order to ensure that they are up to grade. Then I understand when they come to Montreal or Toronto the purchaser is allowed to demand that they be graded again, and that would be done by our man.
The later inspection would be the one counted in the bargain?
Yes. There is an appeal in the trade, and our man sits on that appeal. That would be the last one under the regulations.

I should like to make some inquiries with regard to the grading of poultry in Canada. Is a grade A turkey of the same specifications in Ontario, Saskatchewan and British Columbia? Are the grades dominionwide? Are they agreed to by the provinces and the dominion?

That is the case in the provinces the hon. member has named, but I am not sure that applies to all provinces. It eventually works out that way. When I first came down here Manitoba did not accept the grades in connection with butter, but it was only a short time until they agreed and went along with our arrangement. That is true of most forms of production. Eventually all provinces agree that whatever grades the federal government establishes, they will conform to them.

That is what I understood. When a farmer sells poultry which is graded A or B or whatever it may be, is that grade carried through to the consumer? When a turkey or chicken is purchased from a farmer as grade A and is killed by the packer, is it stamped in such a manner that the consumer knows he is getting a grade A article, the article for which the farmer was paid on a grade A basis. If not, why not?

Of course one can say "yes" to that; one can say that the grade is dominion-wide and that it will probably be adhered to. But then I know my friend would point out to me exactly what happened in Saskatoon at the farmers' union meeting last summer. A chap said: "I took my chickens into such and such a store in Saskatoon last week, they were graded so and so and I was paid so and so. I walked into the store afterwards and saw them being sold, and they were not sold on the same grade or on the same price level at all."
I assume he was telling me the truth, and that comes right back to the fact that there is no way we can enforce that. He would have to get that enforced provincially. There is no way we can enforce it. But in most

Supply-Agriculture
cases throughout the trade and throughout business, when we have sat down and agreed that such and such ought to be the grade and that it ought to be established by the federal government so it will be the same everywhere, most people go along with it and try to carry it out. But if someone undertakes to break it and do something else there is no way we can enforce that kind of thing within a province if the deal is an intraprovincial one.
The minister mentioned a case in Saskatoon where the man took his poultry to a store. They would not be government graded. They would be just graded by the storekeeper.
I did not get that.
I listened to the minister telling the story about the Saskatoon man who took his poultry to a storekeeper. They would not be government graded. The storekeeper would grade them to suit himself.
They would only be what?
I did not hear the minister. I have the same difficulty.
I did not hear the hon. member either through this apparatus.

I think the trouble with these microphones is that when we ask a question they are like a radio; it takes a while for them to warm up. The minister told us about the man who took his poultry to a storekeeper in Saskatoon. The poultry would only be graded by the storekeeper and not by a government grader. Does the minister not think that we should have government graders to protect the farmers in the sale of poultry?

In a country as big as Canada I do not think it would be very practical to have a government grader at every store to which farmers take products. I am afraid that if you started to charge it up to the system there would not be much left either for the producer or consumer by the time we got through with it. There are limits to what you can do with respect to putting inspectors to work. My understanding is that in the province of Ontario the position is established in Toronto, in that regulations with regard to grading are enforced there and are carried out. But the same thing is not done in Saskatoon, and therefore persons there can do something different from what they do in Toronto.

This is the last time I am going to get up on this matter. The minister did a good job during the war so far as grades were concerned. I do not see why he ever quit. He should have kept the thing going

because it was beneficial to both the producer and the consumer, and the minister could have gone one better. Let us go back to turkeys again. When a turkey is graded a ring should be put in its wing to ensure that the consumer will get the same grade the producer got.

We have been talking a lot about government grades and government inspectors, but actually the men who do the grading in the packing plants are paid by the packing plants, are they not? They are really packing plant graders, and the government inspectors merely supervise the general work of the graders. The men who do the actual grading are paid by the packing plants, are they not?
In the plants that are under our inspection-and they are only some of the packing plants in Canada-the men who do the grading are our graders. We hire them and pay them.

Take the packing plants in the west such as Burns, Swift and Canada Packers. Most of the grading of eggs is done by the packing plant graders. I always understood that was the case. Their work is supervised in a general way by inspectors.
I thought the hon. member was talking about hogs and cattle in the packing plants, but if he is still on eggs he is correct.

With respect to poultry, we have specials, grade A, grade B and' grade C. Is there any weight specification involved in these grades? Sometimes you buy a chicken weighing four pounds which is marked grade A. At another time you may buy one weighing six or seven pounds and it is also grade A.
The question of weight is not associated with the grading of poultry. It is a quality grade.

In their presentation to the government this year the Canadian Federation of Agriculture asked for a floor price under poultry. What is the government policy with respect to the establishing of such floor prices?

The main reason for not doing so is that the poultry market is fairly well established. The price suggested by the federation was considerably below the price that farmers are now getting for poultry. There is always a question as to what effect the setting of a support price on a product is going to have. There are some products on which you can have support prices and thereby assist in raising the level of the

return that is going to be received by farmers. There are others where if you do so you can so load up the market that you destroy any market that may exist, particularly when you are confined to your own home market. We have not been altogether confined to our home market, but by far the greater part of our product must be sold here if we are going to sell it at all, and many of the poultry people are of the opinion that the situation is better without a support price than it would be with it.
Does the minister say that the poultry people are satisfied that the market is better off without a floor price?

Yes. I attend the meetings of the federation and I listen to the discussions and the views that are presented there. Before I get to the back of the hall I have a group of fellows parading up to me and saying that the thing is just about right as it is and that we should leave it alone. I have to make up my mind as to where I am getting the best advice. Sometimes I am getting the best advice from the fellows who take that position. Sometimes I get it from the people who pass the resolutions. You have to make up your mind one way or the other as to which group is speaking for the most people. It is not always the people who pass the resolutions. We get our information from many other sources as well.

I do not imagine that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture would pass a resolution unless it represented the considered opinion of the majority of the people in the federation. I would imagine that the reason for their request is not that they are afraid of the price of poultry right now, but that they are afraid of what may happen next October or November when the rush of poultry to the market begins. It might be advisable to have a floor at that time to protect the producers.
If the government in its wisdom saw fit to place a floor under poultry now the producer would have some assurance that he could buy baby chicks a few weeks old now and not have to run the risk of taking a serious loss on them next fall. It would be a guarantee to the producer that he would have a reasonable floor next fall, and on the basis of that floor he could decide whether he should expand or decrease his production.
If we are to have orderly marketing and orderly prices in this country I think there has to be some guarantee to the producer that if he has a product there will be a market and a reasonable floor price. I think it would be a reasonable guarantee to the consumer,
Supply-Agriculture
too, because if the poultry producers at this time get the opinion that next fall there is going to be overproduction, and if they considerably reduce their poultry this summer, then the consumer is going to pay a lot more next fall than he would if production were normal.
I have not discussed this matter with the Canadian Federation of Agriculture but I am sure that in the back of their minds there was the idea of orderly marketing and reasonable production to meet the demands in this country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. I notice from the statistics on the number of cases of eggs purchased by the government that purchases were 39,000 cases out of a production of 5 million cases. I think those figures demonstrate why egg prices went so low. I do not think you can control prices in any market by purchasing less than 1 per cent of the production. There was such a small part of the production purchased, as the farmers' union delegations told us a few weeks ago, that the price of eggs to the producer went down to 27 cents a dozen for grade A large, when it was 40 degrees below zero.
We have producers writing in to say that their eggs have been sold on a non-graded basis at as low as 18 cents a dozen, and some of them lower than that. I agree with the hon. member for Melfort that there should be some floor price, some marketing legislation and some market for poultry products. When I go around to stores in Ottawa and just look in the window and see some of the fowl they have for sale and some of the prices for which they are being sold I am astounded. There is something wrong in the country between the price the producer receives and the price the consumer pays. There is certainly something wrong with the price the producer receives on the prairies and the price the consumer pays in Ontario.
A neighbour showed me her bill of sale for some poultry she sold. The hens were a year old; they had been running around the yard in the summer time; they were not milk fed, but they had all kinds of wheat, oats and barley. The yard was flooded with all kinds of grain. This lady decided to ship the poultry to market and she received a cheque for 31 cents a bird. 1 am sure if one of those birds was purchased in a downtown store it would not be sold for less than $2. There is certainly something wrong when the producer gets just a few cents for the commodity but the consumer pays $2. We certainly need some marketing legislation and

Supply-Agriculture
adequate floor prices. I have here the presentation of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture which says this:
Since it has been apparent that the lower prices being received by our farmers for livestock have not been reflected in the price of meat to the consumer, it is recommended that the federal government take action to investigate, in the interests of the people as a whole, all the elements of cost as between producer and consumer in relation to all meat products.
I think there is certainly a lot of room for investigation when the poultry producers on the prairies are forced out of production because they get practically nothing for their product, yet the consumers see little or no reduction in the price of the products they purchase from the stores. As I understand it, the floor price for eggs is 38 cents a dozen -grade A large coming out of storage-plus 5 cents a dozen for storage charges. If the producer could receive that floor price with perhaps a reduction of 2 cents a dozen for handling the eggs the producer would have an inadequate floor but still a floor price. It seems to me that the packers, in selling to the wholesale houses, their ordinary outlets, must get a considerably higher price or naturally they would sell to the government. It seems to me natural that if they could get 40 cents a dozen in the ordinary retail outlets that is where the eggs would go. When they get 40 cents a dozen apparently the spread is so large that the producer gets only 25 cents a dozen; and I think the federation's request to the cabinet is a good one.
From hearing him speak in the house I am willing to admit that the Minister of Agriculture is a better authority on the constitution of the country than I am or perhaps ever will be, but I would like to see him discuss with the Minister of Justice the constitutionality of adequate marketing legislation; because if there is anything this country needs now, it is some kind of legislation for the control of agricultural products in interprovincial and export trade so the producer may get some kind of guarantee.
I believe it was this afternoon that the minister said Saskatchewan as a province was on the peak, or I believe he called it the roof, of Canada when it came to the matter of eggs. We have a surplus and have to ship them east and west. Freight rates are high and prices are low. The marketing legislation is very inadequate. When the minister says he talks to people at conventions who say they do not want any floors, those people may be right; they do not want any floors when they consider the experience they have had with the floor price on eggs.

I like to see adequate floor prices, but I like to see the producer get the benefit of those floor prices. It seems to me that unless the government has first of all a market for those products, and secondly is prepared to control those products in interprovincial trade, the producer is not going to get much benefit from the floor prices. I would like to know what disposition the government made of the 39,000 cases of eggs it purchased. To whom were they sold and what was the loss on the transaction, although I believe the minister has told us what it was.

Most of the eggs we purchased were sold back into the market in this country, but we sold some to Mexico and some to Venezuela. The loss on the eggs handled was about $53,000.
While I am on my feet I might as well say that I have here a list of the grading stations in Saskatchewan and a list of the prices to the farmers who brought their eggs to those stations throughout the week ending April 18, 1953. The stations fill two pages-
Prices are up now.
-and at only three of those stations were prices down to 35 cents.
Now.
At the others they were 36, 37 and 38 cents. Grade A extra large prices were a little better than that; not very much, but a little better.
Does the minister have the January prices?

I do not know whether we have the January prices, but we will look and see. However, that was the position in the last few weeks. The price levels were just about as I have stated them. As a matter of fact they are the exact price levels. I agree-and I know it to be so- that the farmer is not able to do quite as well where there is no grading station. It goes without saying that two sheets of foolscap would not foe sufficient to set out all the towns, villages and places where there are stores in Saskatchewan and where there are people who sell their eggs at prices lower than those prices. As a matter of fact, there arc; some communities where most of the eggs produced are taken to the store on the old system, traded to the store at a price and traded right out of the store at the same price; and quite often that price is comparatively low. It is used as a means of trading in and out of the store. At the main points where we would have any check, they were 30 cents; at Melville, Regina, Swift Current, Moose Jaw and points of that kind, they were 30 cents.
That is 30 cents for grade A large?
Yes; for grade A large.

What is the difficulty there, when the floor price is 38 cents and the grading stations are paying only 30 cents? Do they need a margin of that kind to operate, in addition to the 5 cents storage payment? They must have had storage facilities at that date because that was early in the egg season.

Yes. The grading, the packing, the packages themselves, the fact that you have got to ship them a certain distance and so on, account for the difference between 30 cents and 38 cents. As a matter of fact, the estimate made in most places at the time the system was first set up was that the margin would be 6 cents. Generally speaking that can still be the case. But in areas such as the Saskatchewan area-partly because it is on the peak, as was stated a few moments ago, and many of the eggs have to be shipped down to Winnipeg or, if they are going west, have to be shipped to Calgary to storage-the costs are greater than they are in most other places; and that adds up to an extra two cents on that particular score.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think this item should be allowed to carry without drawing attention to the type of eggs which are laid in my constituency. I picked up this evening's Ottawa Journal, and I found there an account of how a mother goose, winging desperately to her roost, laid an egg from 800 feet in Mr. Lough's garden but it did not even break. I wonder if such eggs should be sold by weight or by size.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They should be given away.

A paper has just been handed to us here-I see that it is the Ottawa Journal -and I note that grade A turkeys are advertised at 75 cents a pound. I was in the constituency of the Minister of Agriculture last fall. A great many turkeys are raised there. I know the producers there were extremely anxious to get 38 cents a pound, and they were in great doubt whether they would get that much for grade A turkeys.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture has asked the federal government to take action to investigate, in the interests of the people of Canada as a whole, the elements of cost as between producer and consumer in relation to these meat products. What consideration has the Department of Agriculture given to this request by the federation? It seems to me there is no real reason why turkeys should be selling at 75 cents a pound when they were purchased last fall at prices all the way from
Supply-Agriculture
27 to 37 or 38 cents. I think there is need for an investigation. Is the department taking any action with regard to the request of the federation?

Oh, yes. We do check on it. But I would have to get a great deal more information than the hon. member has given me in order to be able to determine whether that is a reasonable relationship. Those turkeys are sold in different ways. Sometimes they are sold with the heads on, the feet on, and so on; sometimes they are sold drawn and sometimes they are not drawn. Whether those turkeys out in Melfort had the heads and feet on and were not drawn, and the others were the other way around, I do not know. I greatly doubt whether my hon. friend knows either. One therefore cannot just talk about turkeys being 38 cents one place and 75 cents another, unless he knows a great deal more about the turkeys than just that.

That is exactly what the Canadian Federation of Agriculture are requesting. They are requesting that some investigation be made with respect to this matter. What I am asking the minister is whether his department is meeting this request of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture by making a real investigation into why there should be such a spread between what the producer receives in certain cases and what the consumer pays. It is certainly the opinion of the farmers that the consumer is paying too much, and the consumer is blaming the producer. I think there is a real field for some investigation and for some definite information. As the minister says, I cannot give that information, nor do I think he can, without a good deal of investigation; and that is what the Canadian Federation of Agriculture are requesting. I think it is a reasonable request.

I might suggest again that it would be much simpler for the government of the province of Saskatchewan to make a check on why the price of turkeys is such and such in Melfort to the farmer and why it is something else when it is sold in town than it would be for this government to go out there and check it for them.
This is in Ontario.
The same thing is true in Ontario. My hon. friend is suggesting that the turkeys were bought out in Melfort and sold in Ontario.
Many of them were.

In so far as that transaction is concerned as between Saskatchewan and here, we have something to do with it and we do make the inspections that have to be made in connection with it. But in so far as the selling of the product in a store in

Supply-Agriculture
the province of Ontario is concerned, the control is under the provincial government, if there is any control on anybody's part, and it depends on whether the provincial government has undertaken the control. Again I say that, so far as I have been able to look into it, they assume just about as much control in Ontario as they do anywhere in Canada.

The minister just mentioned that he would not know whether the turkeys were sold with the feet on or with the heads on or whether they were drawn or were not drawn. I may be wrong, but I think he is in error when he says they could easily be bought with the feet oft, because I think it is illegal to buy turkeys especially with their heads oft; and they have to be drawn after they are purchased so it can be ascertained that they are not diseased.
Where is it illegal?
On any market.
Not in any market. It may be illegal in any market in Ontario.
There are a great many turkeys sold with their heads on.
Is that not true? Is it legal to sell turkeys in the retail trade with their heads oft?

My hon. friend would know far more about that matter in Ontario than I do; and no doubt he can tell me whether or not it is legal. But I would say if it is legal to do it one way or the other, it is enforced by the provincial law.

Apparently the Canadian Federation of Agriculture thought the responsibility for making this investigation lay with the federal government. Did the minister advise them, when they made this presentation, that they should make their request to the provincial government rather than to the federal government, if they wanted an investigation into the spreads in meat prices in Canada?

I was trying to think what it was I had forgotten to tell the hon. member when I was up on my feet before. I am pleased that he has reminded me of it. Every time the federation has come to me since 1948, when we ceased to have authority to do these things, I have told them that they would get along much better and accomplish much more if they went to the provincial governments. The result is that now they do not bother me much about it but they go to the provincial governments.
They made that recommendation?

That is all right. They made that recommendation. They were advised to go to the provincial governments, and they have gone there. They got far more action by going there than they could get here, because that is where the authority is.
I believe the hon. member for Lake Centre asked the minister to give figures regarding the imports of cheese and pork into this country. Has the minister those figures?
I have the exports, but it is a rather long list. I do not happen to have the imports of the products that might come into the country.
The hon. member for Lake Centre could not be here, but the minister promised to give him these figures. I thought this was a good time to get them.

I am sorry; it was around five o'clock when we were discussing them, and there are not very many people around after five o'clock to get us the information. I am not suggesting that it ought to go over until tomorrow morning, but I will get full information and send it to the hon. member, whether we are still on the estimates or not.

I was interested in the minister's remarks on the constitutional question and how the federal government works in this field. Governments have been able to arrive at a satisfactory relationship in the marketing of wheat, oats, barley and other agricultural products. They have controlled the marketing of them, and this policy has been followed out in a manner that is highly satisfactory to the producer. I believe it is the most satisfactory method even so far as the consumers are concerned. If it is constitutional to have a marketing board in the field of grain, why is it not constitutional to make similar arrangements for the marketing of other agricultural products? If you could have a board similar to the wheat board for these other agricultural products you might solve this problem of such large spreads between the producer and the consumer and such highly fluctuating prices from month to month and from year to year. If it is constitutional in one place, why is it not constitutional in the other?

Item agreed to.
33. Subsidies for cold storage warehouses under the Cold Storage Act, and grants, in the amounts detailed in the estimates, $578,729.
In this item there is an amount for the Kensington Dairy Company and in the supplementary estimates there is an estimate for the Crapaud Dairy Company.
I have not the supplementary estimates here at the moment but we shall be coming to them. The Kensington Dairying Co-operative Association is $3,300.
The Crapaud should be about $9,000.
I understand the amount is $9,000; I have not it here at the moment.

Item agreed to.
36. Marketing of agricultural products, including temporary appointments that may be required to be made notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act, the amount available for such appointments not to exceed $6,000.

In the details of this item on page 115 we find: "Advertising and other informational publicity, $92,278." Does the department provide advertising? I always understood that any boards handling agricultural products had to provide their own publicity with regard to the sale of apples, butter and various other products for which we have boards operating. Is any of this grant given for the advertising of particular products?
There is an amount of $92,278 for advertising and other informational publicity. It is exactly the same as it was a year ago. What is the question?
My question is, what particular type of advertising does this cover? Whom is this money paid to?

It is used to advertise the sale of any commodity that we may be handling. The display advertising we had in stores for a while which said "Butter is Better" and that kind of thing would be put out under this item.
This money is spent directly by the department? Grants are not given to other people?
Yes, it is spent directly by the department.
It is only for the sale of products which have been taken over under the Agricultural Prices Support Act.

Not only that. Take the slogan "Butter is Better"; it was a sort of promotional campaign to have people eat butter instead of eating some substitute for it. That was put out all over the country and paid for irrespective of whether we were selling the butter or someone else was selling it.
Was the minister satisfied with the results?

We think we had good results from it. The consumption increased right from the time we started.
Supply-Agriculture
Is it used to advertise canned pork?
Yes, it includes that. We have been advertising it.

What is the intention of the department in relation to the marketing of the 71 million pounds of canned pork? Are you trying to feed it back into the Canadian market, or are you getting rid of some of it in the export market?

We are selling it, I was going to say, all over the world. I do not suppose it is right to say all over the world, but I am told we are selling it broadcast all over the United States. The statement was made to me the other day that in the larger distributing stores in the United States that pork has found its way right down to Texas, which takes us as far south as we can go. Our estimate is that all that pork will go on to that market and the other markets. We are selling smaller amounts of it this year.
What part of the pork is being sold in Canada?

We started out with about 98 million pounds, and we have somewhere around 70 million now. The greater part of what has been sold, to date, has been sold in Canada. However, we have had an advertising and promotional campaign in the United States, and in recent weeks the product has been getting down as far as Texas, and is being sold widely. We expect that by far the greater part of the 70 million pounds will be sold in the United States.
And is the portion sold in the United States sold at the same price that is received here?
Yes, it must be. Otherwise we would get into difficulties in connection with dumping.
What form does the advertising take? I understand the pork is in tins, with the packers' labels on them.

The tin going out bears a Canadian government label. It is a specially made container, different from those in which the other products have gone out. The advertising is done through window streamers and newspapers.
When did you begin using the government label?
About November.
Prior to that it was sold with their own name on it?

Yes.

Supply-Agriculture

Item agreed to.
Terminable services-
37. Freight assistance on western feed grains, $17,000,000.

I notice that this item is headed, "Terminable services". That heading, in itself, is alarming to the eastern consumers of feed grains. Eastern Canada is trying to build up a livestock industry, and they have to depend upon the government from year to year to provide this freight assistance. I know the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in its presentations to the government in the last two or three years has asked that this be made permanent legislation. I believe it has been carried on since 1942, and it has been beneficial to both eastern consumers and western producers.
I suggest that after eleven years we should be able to make up our minds as to whether or not this should be a permanent policy. I would like to see it made permanent. Has the government considered this matter?

This service has been going on since 1941, and has developed into a considerable cost from year to year. I do not know that anything is to be gained by raising the question as to when it will terminate. The matter has been up every year since 1941, and it is still going on. I have concluded in my experiences here that probably one gets into more trouble by raising questions like that than he does by leaving them alone. It has been left alone; it has been accepted from year to year, and I have not heard anyone say it will be stopped. So I am not raising the question myself.

Am I right in stating that the freight rate subsidy has been going down. I may be wrong in my understanding of this, but is it not correct that the freight rate increases are not taken into consideration in connection with the subsidy? Are they not paid on the basis of the old freight rate, with the result that every time there is a new increase, the subsidy is that much less.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is wrong.
It might be possible to show that it has not taken up all the increase. There may be some places where it has not; but it has followed the increase in the upward trend.

Item agreed to.
Terminable services-
39.	To provide for quality premiums on high grade hog carcasses and administration costs, $6,000,000.
Does the government propose any change in the premium paid on hogs, or is it left the same as it was?
We have already announced that for this hog year, which closes at the end of September, there is to be no change. But of course I cannot say beyond that what the position will be.

Item agreed to.
Special
40.	Agricultural products hoard administration, $10,000. '
Is this the item under which the agricultural prices purchase board operates?
Yes.
What amount is made available to the board for purchasing products?
Is the hon. member referring to the agricultural prices support board?
No; I am referring to purchases.

This item does not refer to the agricultural prices support board, but rather to the purchase board which buys any product which may be bought. For instance, when we bought New Zealand butter, it was this board that bought it. Its activities are more limited than those of the agricultural prices support board.

Item agreed to.
Special-
41.	To provide for assistance to encourage the improvement of cheese and cheese factories, $1,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, am I correct in assuming that considerable quantities of various types of cheese, other than common cheddar and other types produced in this country, are imported into Canada? What efforts are being made to develop the manufacture of other types of cheese in this country so that we may be able to supply our own markets?

There are a few organizations which are attempting to produce substitutes for some of the cheeses that come in from European countries and elsewhere, which are a little different from the ordinary run of cheese. There is a church organization in Quebec which makes a certain type of cheese that I buy from time to time and like just as well as a similar looking cheese which comes from Europe. There is another one in Saskatoon which makes a blue coloured cheese which I like very well. There are

plants across the country, but they are not producing in great amount.
On the other hand, there is not a great amount of these varieties of cheese being imported. Taken together they do not amount to a large quantity. Most of the cheese consumed here is Canadian Cheddar and the varieties made from that cheese in spreads or other special forms.

Item agreed to.
Special-
42.	To provide assistance for the replacement of maple production equipment, $300,000.
Who gets this assistance? How much has been paid to each province?

I think I have explained this item every year since about three years before the war. I have said on one or two recent occasions that I think probably we will have to have another look at it one of these times, with the government of Quebec. It is an expenditure that was set up two or three years before the war for the purpose of replacing equipment used in the production of maple syrup and maple products in Quebec, because of the fact that the equipment then in use was placing lead in the maple products with the result that the United States government had taken action against it being shipped into that country.
We undertook to assist the Quebec government in having this equipment changed over to something that would not have a lead covering on it. We have been paying now for some considerable time. The Quebec government does the work; it administers the fund created. Quebec is supposed to put up a third, the farmers are supposed to finance a third themselves, and we finance the remaining third. While we do not say this could happen only in Quebec, nevertheless Quebec is the only place where it has operated.

Item agreed to.
44. Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and water storage, $3,750,000.

Can the minister tell us about a P.F.R.A. development near Plum Coulee. This is not in my constituency, but some friends there wrote and asked me to find out about it. I took the matter up with the department and found out that this project evidently was started in 1936 and there was some preliminary work done up to 1939.
The important point in regard to this dam is that the creek drops about 40 feet to the mile and a dam 500 feet long and 40 feet high would be required to hold the water. The
Supply-Agriculture
cost would be in the neighbourhood of $100,000 under present construction conditions, which may perhaps be high in relation to the quantity of water that would be stored. Is this work being proceeded with or is it considered not to be feasible? I have never been near the place at which the dam is expected to be built, but I have been at Morden and saw the dam which was built there under P.F.R.A. and I consider it a wonderful piece of work.

A proposal has been made to have a dam built at this point but it is just in the investigational stage and I have no complete report on it. It has not yet been determined that a dam can be built there, and we have made no preparations for doing so.
I think the survey was started in 1936 and completed in 1938, and then the war years came along. I think some work was done around 1950.
Does the hon. member know the name by which it is known? There is no dam at Plum Coulee.
The officials know, because I have taken it up with them.
We have a long list of dam construction works in western Canada, and there is no Plum Coulee dam.
It is under 625 in Manitoba.
The hon. member should come well armed with information when he starts talking about dams in this house.
The minister is prepared if I can have the name of the dam.
Perhaps it would save time if the minister looked it up and then either sent me the information or told me tomorrow.
This is the item under which the South Saskatchewan dam would be built if it is ever built?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item 45 covers major irrigation projects in the prairie provinces.
Would this vote cover British Columbia?
The P.F.R.A. does not apply to British Columbia. There are special votes covering activities in British Columbia, No. 47 being one.
Has the minister a list of the major projects that it is expected to carry forward, and the money being voted here for each?

Item agreed to.
45. Major irrigation and reclamation projects in the prairie provinces, $7,893,420.

Mr. Chairman, since this is the item under which the South Saskatchewan dam could be built, how can the minister in good conscience suggest to the government of Saskatchewan that they forward him proposals for building the South Saskatchewan dam when there is no item in the estimates under which that could be undertaken? There are a few hundred thousand dollars, but it has been getting less and less every year. The supplementary estimates are in and no money is provided there. The session will soon be over. I suppose an agreement could be made next week and the minister would still be all right, at least for one more year, because he would not have any money to do anything with anyway.
Of the $7,893,420 there is an amount that it is understood would be there for the South Saskatchewan if it were necessary to expend it, and that amount is $1 million.
It is not in there.

It is in there if you look in the right place. The arrangement that was agreed to was that the amount would be left the same as it was last year in so far as the understandings between the department and the treasury were concerned, and the amount last year was $1 million. The total amount of the vote is higher this year than it was last year; it is $7,893,420 as against $7,564,630. To say there is not any money there is just-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Just saying the truth.
-going on saying what my hon. friends have been saying all the time; anything that suits them, they say.

I wonder if I could ask the Minister of Finance a question. Is this item of $500,000 correct, or should it be $1 million? If it should be, will the minister move that it be increased to $1 million. We are passing the items printed in the estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The item is $7,893,420. All of that, if they wanted to, could be used for the South Saskatchewan.

Oh, no, it could not. Of the $7,800,000 there is $3,400,000 for Bow river and $1 million for the St. Mary irrigation project. The only amounts here that could be used on the South Saskatchewan are represented by the items that are labelled

"South Saskatchewan", and they total $636,000 compared with $2 million before the last general election.
Who is going to stop them?

It is just one-third as much as we had in 1949. Instead of getting closer to the project we are getting farther away from it. If we had a pretty good chance of the project being started in 1949, we are down to one-third of that chance tonight.

All I want to add is that if you can convince the people of Saskatchewan that there is no money you will probably not get the dam, but I am going to spend my time trying to convince them that there is some money.
Oh, oh.

Money or no money.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
